articles.title: To Putin’s delight: Politicians in Poland and Ukraine are stoking mutual hostility for the sake of their ratings
articles.body:
In early 2022, when Russian tanks were massed outside Kyiv, Poland proved to be one of Ukraine’s most reliable and steadfast allies. But four years later, relations have entered a crisis — one fueled by historical grievances and economic disputes. Today, 52% of Poles are opposed to their country supporting Ukraine’s accession to the EU, while 44% favor suspending military aid. Politicians on both sides of the border are actively exploiting these disagreements to boost their own ratings, forgetting about the strategic partnership. Meanwhile, Russia is gleefully fanning the flames of the dispute, Polish commentator Pavel Reshka writes.
Family quarrels
What is happening today at the level of the Polish and Ukrainian governments sometimes resembles a kindergarten sandbox squabble. For example, Polish politicians recently began competing over who had sent less military equipment to Ukraine.
“We gave them nothing but scrap metal from our warehouses!” says a former prime minister.
“Scrap metal? It was pretty good weaponry! I’ll show everyone the documents now! Here we are! We’re hardly giving them anything,” counters the former defense minister.
“What about the Patriot missiles?” the opposition presses.
Under normal circumstances, a cabinet minister would be proud of having sent missiles to save the lives of countless innocent civilians by protecting Ukraine from Russia’s barbaric attacks. But now this is not a source of pride, but a political problem — something that requires defensive justification.
Or take the Ukrainian president naming a Ukrainian Armed Forces unit after the “heroes of the UPA.” This, in fact, was the initial trigger of the current escalation. Volodymyr Zelenskyy showed complete disregard for the fact that the reaction in Poland would be fierce, as the awful role of the WWII-era Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) in the Volhynia Massacre represents a historical wound that has still not healed. When pollsters ask Poles, “What should the government discuss with Ukraine?” they hear in response: the exhumation and commemoration of the thousands of compatriots killed by the UPA in 1943, who still lie in the ground in mass graves on the other side of the border.
Moves like Zelensky's provoke outrage. Polish President Karol Nawrocki, egged on by pro-Russian politicians such as former Prime Minister Leszek Miller, demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy be stripped of the Order of the White Eagle. (gov.pl)
Zelensky did not keep him waiting long, sending it back to Nawrocki by mail in a box, and several former Ukrainian presidents, cabinet ministers, ambassadors, and officials followed suit with their Polish awards. Suddenly, a multitude of Orders of the White Eagle arrived in Poland. In the opposite direction, Polish officials sent Orders of Prince Yaroslav the Wise, 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Class.
Warsaw is not at the table during “Coalition of the Willing” meetings — at Kyiv’s behest — nor is it part of the newly formed anti-ballistic coalition.
“Fine! We don’t care. And you’re not getting into the EU with your Bandera anyway,” the Poles say.
“You don’t care? Well, did you know Zelensky won’t be coming to Gdańsk?”
“But it’s the Ukraine Recovery Conference!”
“We can handle the recovery without you as well.”
Online, the two sides are trading blows. Experts and analysts on the Polish side are sounding the alarm that Ukraine is steeped in Nazism and Bandera ideology. Ukrainian experts insist that the atmosphere in Poland is reminiscent of the period before pogroms. They call on fellow citizens living along the Vistula to return home (which makes sense, since Ukraine has an interest in having its citizens return, just as Polish business owners have an interest in having them stay in Poland).
It should be noted here that the Polish police respond firmly and in an exemplary manner to reports of physical aggression against Ukrainians (these are orders from above). However, anti-Ukrainian and anti-Polish sentiment is currently in vogue – it generates clicks and likes.
The conflict has gone so far that Przemysław Czarnek, a leading politician in Poland’s main opposition party, Law and Justice (PiS), and a potential candidate for prime minister, declares: “We need to force the European Union, including by using our position within the EU, to suspend all funding for arms deliveries to Ukraine and for Ukraine’s reconstruction for the time being, until it sets out on the path of universal human values.”
True, Czarnek was called to order by the party chairman and the party split — not surprising given that PiS is not some fringe group, but the main opposition party. It was PiS that was running Poland in 2022 and did everything it could to help its neighbors. Its political position has always been to support Ukraine’s sovereignty and exercise caution toward imperial Russia. Its ranks produced the late Lech Kaczyński, who addressed the parliament in Tbilisi in 2008, with Russian tanks stationed on the outskirts of the city: “Today Georgia, tomorrow Ukraine, the day after tomorrow the Baltic states, and then perhaps the time will come for my country, Poland!” Now, one of the leading figures in the PiS of 2026 is calling for the suspension of Western aid to Kyiv.
Pendulum: from love to hatred
Amid the flurry of mutual accusations, several fundamental problems are being overlooked. Ukraine is fighting a defensive war. At such a moment, its only concern is the struggle for survival. When you are fighting for your life, there is no room for any phrase beginning with “yes, but…” There are no nuances when the world is burning, bombs are falling on your head, and the eastern horde is taking yet another village.
There are no nuances when the world is burning, bombs are falling on your head, and the eastern horde is taking yet another city
Poland is Ukraine’s closest ally. Whatever politicians and commentators in Warsaw may say, it is a weapons supplier and the logistical backbone of the front.
The two countries have a common existential enemy, and Ukraine’s defeat would be a catastrophe for Poland’s security. Ukraine’s victory and its continued course toward the West are crucial to that security, but Ukraine will not ever be able to join the EU without Poland’s consent. And glorifying historical figures who are, to put it mildly, controversial, certainly does not help Kyiv's cause. More than a million Ukrainians live, work, study, and pay taxes in Poland. Despite the disagreements, we are neighbors. And as we can see, despite the Kremlin’s enormous efforts, that is not going to change.
In the words of Jerzy Giedroyc, whose ideas became the foundation of Poland’s foreign policy after 1989:
“Polish state interests require a belt of independent states between Poland and Russia. Warsaw should support the sovereignty of its eastern neighbors, even if this means giving up some historical claims and disputes. Historical conflicts with Ukrainians should not obscure the strategic goal – an independent Ukraine as a guarantee of Poland’s security against Russian imperialism.”
So what, then, is the problem? Well, if you look at it coldly and armed with statistics, there is nothing surprising about the current dispute. CBOS, one of Poland’s most important public opinion research centers, first asked respondents about their attitudes toward Ukrainians in 1993. At the time, just 12% of Poles expressed sympathy for their neighbors, while a full 65% of respondents expressed dislike. Even Russians, Germans, and Jews – nations that traditionally receive only “so-so” affection in Poland – elicited warmer feelings. One could say that Poles really enjoyed not liking Ukrainians back then. A year later, in 1994, sympathy fell even further, reaching a historic low of 9%.
And all this was happening at a time when the Third Polish Republic was proud that “Solidarity” had helped bring down the USSR – the evil empire. In Warsaw, the independence gained by every nation recently subjugated under Moscow's rule was greeted with applause. On a diplomatic level, Poland was, after all, the first country to recognize Ukraine’s independence. The ideas of Jerzy Giedroyc described above were the guiding principle of its eastern policy, even if the mood in society was less than enthusiastic about befriending their newly free neighbor.
Interestingly, in the years that followed, sympathy toward Ukrainians and Ukraine slowly grew — albeit in an up-and-down pattern resembling a sine wave creeping upward. Surges of warm feelings came at particular moments. Poles felt warmly toward their neighbors in 2004 during the Orange Revolution, in 2008 at the time of the Russian-Georgian war, and in 2013–2014 during Ukraine's Revolution of Dignity, Russia's annexation of Crimea, and the outbreak of war in Donbas. Each upswing was followed by a cooling-off period, usually caused by fatigue with the situation and the return of difficult questions about history, particularly the war crimes committed by the UPA in Volhynia.
For a long time, Ukrainian politicians considered the UPA issue to be a problem invented for the purposes of domestic politics in Poland. However, as all the studies show, this is a deep wound that cannot be ignored. In 1943, at least 100,000 innocent civilians were killed in mass killings organized by the UPA. They were murdered in brutal ways. To this day, many Poles believe that the matter has not been properly resolved, and it cannot be buried without exhumations and re-burials. Ukraine blocked a decision on this for years.
The killing of 100,000 Polish civilians by the UPA cannot be resolved without exhumations and burials, and Ukraine blocked a decision on this for years
Thus, Poles' sympathy for their neighbors rose and fell. However, the pendulum never returned to its previous position, and from decade to decade, Poles grew increasingly fond of Ukrainians. By around 2010, sympathy had even begun to outweigh antipathy.
Sentiments on the other side of the border were similar. This is only natural: when we are in trouble, we appreciate a neighbor who wants to come to our aid, and we are grateful to them. Polish flags on the Maidan, the visit of Presidents Lech Kaczyński and Viktor Yushchenko to Tbilisi in 2008, Warsaw’s protests against the brazen annexation of Crimea – all this made a favorable impression on Ukrainians.
A pattern is easy to spot here: the worse Russian behavior was, the better relations between Poles and Ukrainians became. From this perspective, their attachment was a function of their dislike of an aggressive neighbor that threatened “both you and us.” A similar mechanism came into play in 2022. Poles opened their homes and hearts, taking in hundreds of thousands of women and children fleeing the full-scale war unleashed by the Kremlin.
President Andrzej Duda, the PiS government, and the opposition alike did everything they could to provide civilians with social assistance and the Ukrainian army with weapons and ammunition. However, the wave of spontaneous empathy and outrage at Russia, which was committing war crimes, did not prevent Polish politicians from keeping an eye on sociological trends. They could see that if Ukraine survived, the pendulum of sympathy would begin to swing in the other direction, and they needed to prepare for that.
Sociologists say that 2022 was nevertheless such an extraordinary year that it completely disrupted the typical pattern on both sides of the border. CBOS polls show that in March of that year, 94% of Poles supported accepting refugees from Ukraine, and Poland was Ukrainians’ most favored country, with 83% expressing a positive opinion of Poles. President Zelensky said that Ukraine and Poland were sisters.
It must be said that sister Poland really did open its arms wide to sister Ukraine. Legislators in Warsaw changed laws with lightning speed: for example, the law on assistance to Ukrainian citizens was adopted as early as March 12, 2022. This allowed refugees to easily legalize their stay and establish lives thanks to access to the labor market, social assistance, health care, and education – around 300,000 children and teenagers who did not know the language entered the school system. The challenge was enormous: during the first two weeks after February 24 alone, around a million people crossed the Polish border. Europe had not seen such a mass movement since World War II.
And estimates of the size of the migration varied considerably. For example, according to the Union of Polish Metropolises, shortly after the invasion there could have been as many as 3.9 million Ukrainians in Poland.
Reality and emotions
A year and a half later, more precise estimates could be made. They showed that the number of Ukrainians in Poland with an active PESEL Ukr number (which confirms legal residence and grants access to social benefits) stood at around 970,000. The majority of them (87%) were women and children. Poland is also home to more than 420,000 Ukrainians residing on other grounds, including temporary residence related to employment and permanent residence. This puts the total at approximately 1.4 million.
Sister Ukraine actively got to work in Poland. A year and a half after the invasion, 80% of Ukrainian migrant households supported themselves through their own labor. They worked for others or started businesses themselves: since 2022, Ukrainians have founded 60,000 businesses, of which around 35,000 remain active. They also own or co-own the largest share of companies with foreign capital (41%). “Ukrainian workers contributed to higher economic growth, by between 0.7 and 1.1 percentage points,” says Aleksander Łaszek, PhD in economics and a Deloitte expert.
Sister Poland, however, was in shock. After World War II, our country was essentially mono-ethnic. According to the 2011 National Census, foreigners accounted for only 0.1–0.2% of Poland’s population, or about 60,000 people. In reality, the figure was probably closer to 100,000, but hearing another language on the street was something unusual. In recent years, everything has been turned upside down: Ukrainian, and less often Russian and Belarusian, can be heard in stores, hospitals, and hotels. This could not fail to provoke a reaction from a society unprepared for such a dramatic change, and its effects were bound to begin showing up in the polls.
According to the 2011 National Population Census, foreigners accounted for around 0.1–0.2% of Poland’s population
Symptoms of the unraveling solidarity appeared fairly early. “What united the narratives of our middle- and working-class respondents was a strong dislike of Ukrainians, expressed spontaneously in all the focus groups. They reflect anxiety about losing priority access to benefits and public services,” Przemysław Sadura and Sławomir Sierakowski wrote in their report "Poles Are for Ukraine, but Against Ukrainians," based on research conducted in early June 2022.
Such voices rarely broke through into public discourse, but in real life people increasingly talked, for example, about Ukrainians driving down wages. The actual data showed that this was not true. For example, the influx of migrants had a negligible effect on the rise in unemployment (0.18–0.3%), and as Dr. Łaszek noted, “A Ukrainian taking a job was often associated with a Polish worker being promoted because they were more experienced and had a better command of the language.”
However, some rumors cannot be disproved with hard economic data. How, for example, do you disprove the panicked rumors about cunning Ukrainian women who, instead of showing gratitude, set about seducing Polish husbands? Or about Ukrainian children being admitted to emergency departments (SORs) ahead of young Poles waiting in line? These stories spread on social media, and according to experts, they were part of a disinformation campaign – one of many that would later sweep across Poland.
Of course, there were also measurable, entirely objective factors. Ukraine, having gained easier access to EU markets for grain and transportation because of the ongoing war, became a genuine competitor to Polish farmers and businesses. This resulted in a huge influx of grain into Poland, falling prices, and farmers’ protests in 2023, accompanied by a blockade of the border and Ukrainian grain being dumped onto the ground – images that were particularly painful in Ukraine, which had experienced the Holodomor.
This was compounded by President Zelensky’s words at a UN session: “Some of our friends are helping to set the stage for a Moscow actor.” In Poland, this was perceived as a stab in the back to President Andrzej Duda, who was finding it increasingly difficult to rally his camp behind unconditional support for Ukraine.
Moreover, Ukraine was putting pressure on EU institutions, arguing that the restrictions were hurting its economy and violating the principles of the single market and trade agreements. The European Commission became an arena for the dispute, as it was the Commission that administered the so-called autonomous trade measures for Ukraine. In September 2023, after the Commission decided not to extend the EU ban on imports, Ukraine filed a complaint against Poland (and also against Hungary and Slovakia) at the WTO.
In Poland, this was seen as disloyalty and a lack of solidarity. After all, it was not only Andrzej Duda who might have disliked Zelensky’s barbed hint at him in his UN speech. The late Lech Kaczyński must have felt awful when his friend Viktor Yushchenko called Stepan Bandera and Roman Shukhevych heroes. And Bronisław Komorowski must have felt the same when, on the day he addressed the Verkhovna Rada, Ukrainian lawmakers passed a law granting UPA fighters veteran status.
Foreign policy as domestic policy
Poland entered an electoral cycle in 2023, beginning with parliamentary elections marked by the highest turnout in the country's history. This was followed by the no less hotly contested presidential election of 2025. In 2027 there will once again be a battle for a parliamentary majority, a fact that does not make for normal debate.
Parties commission polls and tailor their messaging to voters’ expectations, and a combination of fear and anxiety can propel a party to the top. Everyone wants to ride this wave; no one will swim against the current, because they will drown.
“Of course, politicians sensed the growing skepticism and did not want to go against the tide,” political scientist Ernest Wyciszkiewicz, until recently the director of the Juliusz Mieroszewski Center for Dialogue, said in an interview with Polityka weekly. The center has been conducting detailed sociological research on Polish-Ukrainian relations since the beginning of the invasion, and historical issues — Volhynia, exhumations, and irritation over monuments being erected and streets being named after figures such as UPA commander Roman Shukhevych — have been coming up increasingly often.
On the Ukrainian side, meanwhile, there has been a noticeable rise in national pride. There has also been a renaissance of interest in history. Under the circumstances of the war, the past actions of the UPA have been reinterpreted. Just a decade and a half ago, only around 20% of respondents viewed the UPA positively. Today, the overwhelming majority viewing them as fighters for independence. More than 80% sympathize with Stepan Bandera, and around 70% with Roman Shukhevych, both of whom are viewed as villains in Poland.
More than 80% of Ukrainians sympathize with Bandera, and around 70% with Shukhevych
Poles do not like this, but this is perhaps the worst possible moment to give their neighbors “history lessons.” Ukrainians are defending themselves against Russia and suffering daily casualties. They have no desire to listen to criticism from anyone.
At the same time, far-right groups have been gaining popularity in Poland by riding the anti-Ukrainian wave. A party called “Confederation” received 7% and 18 seats in parliament in October 2023, finishing fifth. Today, “Confederation” has split into two factions, both of which are gaining ground: the first has around 13–15% support, while the second has around 8–11%. In the presidential election, candidates from “Confederation” came in third and fourth, while the top spot went to PiS candidate Karol Nawrocki, a former head of the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) who had no qualms about attacking “Banderite” Ukraine, threatening that it would not join NATO or the EU and calling for the “restoration of justice” – that is, stripping refugees of financial benefits.
The radicals’ convictions inevitably set the tone of the debate, leading others to become more radical. As a result, a law was passed abolishing assistance for the most vulnerable Ukrainian refugees who depend on aid. It is not about the money (after all, it is a pittance), but about showing that we care primarily about our own citizens. The prime minister talks about the need to deport young Ukrainians who got into a scuffle with security guards at a concert (by Max Korzh in Warsaw), while the interior minister personally takes up the case of a blogger who drove a race car with Ukrainian license plates into a national park in the Tatra Mountains to take a selfie. The illegal catching of a catfish by a Ukrainian migrant is elevated to the level of a national security issue.
Ukraine, too, pretends that it is not engaged in domestic politics amid the war, but that is not true either. A political game is afoot in Kyiv given the understanding that as soon as the shooting stops, parliamentary elections and a new race for the presidency will begin.
A Ukrainian opposition politician said that viewing the current dispute with Poland as a cunning ploy by Zelensky would be a gross exaggeration: “There is a narrative being promoted in Warsaw that Zelensky cleverly engineered all this – he stirred up a storm and boosted his ratings. That is a wonderful compliment to the president’s entourage, but completely undeserved. There was no plan. It should be added that, like a stage performer, he has a genius for reading his audience. He quickly realized that people liked this assertiveness and went in that direction: ‘Karol wants the White Eagle back? Great, send it!’ And he was right. The support was enormous. Unfortunately, the price was a deterioration in relations with Poland.”
Zelensky went further, pushing through a law on the Pantheon of Heroes of Ukraine. It is to be a place commemorating figures important to the country’s history and will almost certainly include people whom Warsaw will find difficult to accept. Kyiv, for example, is seeking the return of Stepan Bandera’s remains to Ukraine, to be followed by a ceremonial burial. Even politicians who are not sympathetic to Zelensky came out in his support.
Zelensky is, after all, fighting for reelection. A huge corruption scandal is hanging over him, and increasingly serious opponents are emerging. The situation at the front, dissatisfaction with mobilization, and holes in the budget are all on his shoulders. Relations with Poland are certainly not a priority for him. Preserving his hold on power, however, is.
Nothing but negativity
The Polish research group Res Futura, which studies the internet and social media, noticed something interesting during the latest dispute over naming a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA.” According to its research, 754,000 posts about Ukraine appeared from June 1-21, 2026. These posts generated 10.2 million reactions and comments. “Among non-neutral posts, nine out of ten are negative toward Ukrainians,” emphasized Michał Fedorowicz of Res Futura.
Between June 1 and 21, 2026, 754,000 posts about Ukraine appeared, and if neutral posts are excluded, nine out of ten are negative, Res Futura calculated
Criticism of Ukraine on social media has been growing steadily since the beginning of May, and each crisis pushes this level higher. Importantly, it no longer recedes.
Fedorowicz says that the UPA issue accounted for less than 5% of discussions about Ukraine on social media a year ago. At the time, there was a social and online consensus that the issue should not be discussed because it served Russia’s interests (and was being promoted by pro-Russian propaganda). However, the situation has now been turned upside down: “Today, there is absolutely no room – above all, politically – to change these sentiments.”
Of course, eventually, the pendulum will swing in the other direction again – the sooner, the better. At some point, Poland and Ukraine will love each other a little more again – they have little choice. That is, after all, how sisters love.

articles.title: South Korea president stresses US alliance as many baffled by Trump order to cut exercises
articles.body:
South Korea president stresses US alliance as many baffled by Trump order to cut exercises
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — South Korea’s president said Tuesday a solid alliance with the United States underpins national security, after U.S. President Donald Trump’s abrupt order to “substantially reduce” joint military exercises left many many South Koreans baffled and concerned.
Trump made the surprise announcement in a social media post just before U.S. and South Korean soldiers began Monday’s annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, which are largely designed to sharpen readiness against North Korean threats.
Trump cited what he said was a good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korea’s refusal to join the U.S. war against Iran.
Trump’s move was apparently taken without consultations with South Korea and meant to reach out to Kim, deepening concerns about the reliability of the U.S.-South Korean alliance forged in the turmoil of the 1950-53 Korean War.
A weakening of the U.S. defense commitment could shake South Korea’s national security as it has no nuclear weapons and is under the U.S. “nuclear umbrella” protection, which guarantees a devastating American response in the event of an attack on its ally by nuclear-armed North Korea. The U.S. has about 28,500 troops in South Korea.
Confidence in the U.S. has already eroded among many South Koreans because of Trump’s tariff war and last year’s immigration raid in the U.S. state of Georgia that led to the detention of hundreds of South Korean workers.
Trump’s announcement “reveals the stark reality of a faltering Korea-U.S. alliance, fueling public anxiety,” South Korea’s Hankook Ilbo newspaper said in an editorial Tuesday. “It’s absurd that the U.S. appears to treat North Korea more respectfully than its ally South Korea.”
South Korean leader calls for solid US alliance
In a regular Cabinet meeting, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung stressed the importance of a firm military alliance with the U.S., saying that “national security will be further strengthened when the alliance is solid.”
“When we build up our strengths, our value and importance as an ally will further grow,” said Lee, a liberal who has called for a stronger, self-reliant defense posture.
It was unclear which parts of the 11-day South Korea-U.S. exercises were being downsized. The South Korean and U.S. militaries earlier said their drills this year would be similar in scale to previous years and incorporate lessons from recent conflicts such as North Korea’s battlefield experiences on the Russia-Ukraine front. They also said the drills are defensive in nature.
North Korea’s Foreign Ministry accused South Korea and the U.S. of plotting more provocative drills this year and vowed to respond with “a new level of a deterrent.”
Prospects unclear for reengagement between Trump and Kim
Kim has shunned any talks with the U.S. and South Korea since his earlier high-profile diplomacy with Trump fell apart in 2019.
Experts say Kim won’t likely embrace Trump’s overture and return to talks anytime soon unless he is promised bigger U.S. concessions. Kim has boosted his military and diplomatic credentials in recent years by enlarging his nuclear arsenal and aligning with Russia over its war against Ukraine.
Lee’s presidential office on Monday expressed hopes that a “friendly relationship” between Trump and Kim would lead to “meaningful dialogue” between their countries to promote peace on the Korean Peninsula. That invited a backlash from conservatives, who criticized Lee’s government for allegedly prioritizing resumption of Kim-Trump diplomacy over security concerns.
“South Korea’s security bulwark is being shaken to its very foundations,” Park Chung-kwon, a spokesperson for the main conservative opposition People Power Party, said in a statement.
Doubts about US alliance grow in South Korea
In his social media post, Trump said the military exercises with South Korea are not only costly but “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea, which he said “has been unthreatening and respectful” during his time in the White House. Trump said he asked Lee if South Korea would join the U.S. in the “denuclearization” of Iran, “and they said, ‘No thanks!’”
Lee’s office said South Korea and the U.S. are closely discussing practical and military contributions that South Korea can make to help restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
“Trump thinks of an alliance as an investment that should pay regular dividends, or a rainy-day fund he can withdraw from when another project isn’t going well,” said Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
“South Korean leaders understand that relations with the Trump administration will be a constant renegotiation linking economic and security issues. Seoul is thus cautiously responding to recent developments within that framework,” Easley said.

articles.title: Beyond Syria: Russia's role in the Middle East enters a new era
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Beyond Syria: Russia's role in the Middle East enters a new era
When Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani toured Hmeimim airbase and Tartus port on 9 August, the images offered a striking reversal of the relationship Syria had known under Bashar Al-Assad.
In footage widely circulated after the visit, Syrian officials walked through facilities that had once embodied Moscow's dominance over its ally.
Under a new memorandum of understanding, Damascus will assume control of civilian facilities at Hmeimim and the commercial section of Tartus, while Russia's remaining military installations will be reorganised as joint training and capacity-building centres.
The agreement, reached after 18 months of negotiations, gives the two sides three months to complete the transition. Russian personnel will remain at the new centres, although neither government has disclosed their number or the precise military activities Moscow will be allowed to conduct.
For Damascus, the arrangement restores sovereignty over strategic infrastructure surrendered to Russia under Assad. For Moscow, however, it also avoids the outcome the Kremlin feared after Assad's fall in December 2024: losing Syria altogether.
What emerges is therefore a much smaller Russian presence, negotiated with rather than imposed on Damascus. Its importance, however, extends beyond Syria. Hmeimim and Tartus remain part of the infrastructure connecting Russia to the Mediterranean, Libya, and its expanding military presence in Africa.
From military bases to negotiated access
Russia’s intervention in Syria in 2015 transformed Hmeimim and Tartus into the backbone of its regional military posture. Hmeimim supported Russian air operations across Syria, while Tartus provided the navy with its only Mediterranean repair and replenishment facility.
Those privileges rested on agreements concluded with Assad that gave Moscow extraordinary freedom of operation. The new arrangement effectively replaces that relationship with one in which access depends on Syrian consent.
The military drawdown, however, began long before the August agreement. In the weeks after Assad’s fall, Russian forces withdrew from secondary positions around Manbij, Kobane, Palmyra and Qamishli, concentrating personnel and equipment at Hmeimim and Tartus before moving substantial quantities out of Syria.
By late January 2025, Russian cargo vessels were removing vehicles and other materiel accumulated at Tartus, while the last Russian submarine in the Mediterranean had already departed through Gibraltar on 2 January.
Major capabilities that had previously protected Russia’s Syrian deployment also disappeared. Anton Mardasov, a Russia and Syria specialist at the Middle East Institute, recently told The New Arab that Moscow had withdrawn almost all its major weapons systems by January 2025, including S-300 and S-400 air-defence systems.
The sequence matters. In mid-December, Russian aircraft, helicopters and fighters were still visible at Hmeimim, while S-300 and S-400 systems were being repositioned westwards as Moscow consolidated its remaining forces. Their subsequent withdrawal was therefore part of a progressive contraction rather than an immediate abandonment of Syria after Assad’s fall.
According to Nanar Hawach, a senior Syria analyst at the International Crisis Group, “the actual blow to Russia’s position happened with Assad's fall in December 2024, and everything since has reduced its presence to what Damascus is willing to host”.
The August memorandum formalises that transformation. Russia retains access, but the bases no longer provide the regional deterrence and freedom of action they once did.
Why Damascus still wants Moscow
The new Syrian government has little reason to restore Russia’s former position, but it also has little incentive to sever relations completely.
President Ahmed al-Sharaa has pursued that balance since taking power. During his first meetings with Russian officials in January 2025, he called for relations to address Moscow’s role in the Syrian war and respect Syrian sovereignty. Damascus has also demanded the extradition of Assad, who remains in Russia and was sentenced to death in absentia by a Syrian court on 11 August.
Yet al-Sharaa has visited Moscow twice, while Russian and Syrian delegations have continued discussing military cooperation, reconstruction and trade.
Russia retains leverage through areas in which replacing it quickly would be difficult. Syria's military still relies heavily on Soviet- and Russian-origin equipment, while Moscow remains an important supplier of wheat and energy.
Russian oil deliveries reportedly reached around 60,000 barrels per day by May, after Syria lost access to Iranian supplies following Assad’s fall. Russia has also supplied much of Syria’s imported wheat.
Damascus is already seeking alternatives. Syrian officials have reportedly told Washington that they are prepared to sharply reduce Russian oil imports as part of negotiations over Syria’s removal from the US state sponsors of terrorism list.
The same approach is visible at Tartus. Syria cancelled the Assad-era contract with Russian company STG Stroytransgaz to operate the commercial port in January 2025 and later signed an $800 million agreement with Dubai-based DP World.
But reducing dependence does not require excluding Moscow. Russian companies are discussing renewed commercial cooperation, and the Russian-Syrian Business Council is planning a business forum in November involving around 50 Russian companies, with sectors ranging from agriculture and energy to construction materials.
Russia’s realistic role may therefore be less about financing Syria's reconstruction than supplying commodities, maintaining Soviet-era infrastructure and military equipment, and offering services that Damascus can use while other partners enter the country.
A smaller footprint, from Syria to Libya
The transformation becomes clearer when Syria is viewed alongside Russia’s expanding position in Libya. As Russian forces contracted their Syrian deployment after Assad’s fall, transport aircraft began flying between Hmeimim and al-Khadim airbase in eastern Libya. An-124 and Il-76 aircraft were used in what appeared to be a substantial logistical transfer, while Russian activity also increased at other Libyan installations.
That network has since expanded. Russian personnel linked to the Africa Corps are now operating or developing infrastructure at al-Khadim, al-Jufra, al-Qardabiyah, Brak al-Shati, Tamanhint and Maaten al-Sarra. The latter, close to Chad and Sudan, gives Moscow a particularly useful staging point for operations further into Africa.
Libya is nevertheless an imperfect replacement for Syria. Its ports lack some of the infrastructure Russia enjoyed at Tartus, while access depends on local political relationships rather than sovereign Russian control.
This may explain the model now emerging. “Instead of having a naval air base in the eastern Mediterranean, Russia could end up with facilities for its fleet in Syria, at Tartus, and in Libya, for its air force,” Igor Delanoë, deputy director of the Franco-Russian Observatory, told The New Arab.
“This represents a lighter footprint, the very nature of which is both a strength and a weakness,” he said. Russia would face a lower political cost if it were forced out, but its access could also “easily be suspended or even terminated by the Syrian or Libyan side”.
The growing reliance on multiple access points also reflects the wider geography in which Moscow sees its Mediterranean presence. Laetitia Meenen, a researcher focusing on Russia’s relations with the Gulf and Middle East, argues that Tartus remains valuable because it sits along a broader route connecting the Black Sea and Mediterranean with the Red Sea and Indian Ocean.
“Tartus is a crucial military base for Russia, enabling it to project its naval power in the Mediterranean and beyond,” Meenen told The New Arab. “Russia is also seeking access to ports in the Red Sea, such as Port Sudan, to expand its influence.”
For Delanoë, Moscow is therefore likely to continue diversifying its support points, including through naval stopovers in Algeria and its long-running effort to secure access on Sudan's Red Sea coast.
Russia's Mediterranean presence is reduced, but not finished
That diversification has become more important because Russia's naval position in the Mediterranean has deteriorated dramatically. For the first time in more than a decade, Moscow currently lacks the permanently deployed combat force that characterised its Mediterranean posture after the intervention in Syria.
The Mediterranean Operational Squadron that once allowed Russia to shadow NATO deployments, sustain operations in Syria and maintain Kalibr-capable ships and submarines in the region has effectively disappeared.
Delanoë cautions against interpreting this as permanent. “The Russian naval presence has diminished but has not disappeared,” he told The New Arab, pointing to two constraints: Russia’s loss of control over Tartus and Turkey’s closure of the Turkish Straits to belligerent warships under the Montreux Convention since February 2022.
If the war in Ukraine ends and the Straits reopen, he expects Russian naval deployments to resume more regularly. “I believe the Mediterranean naval detachment will return, in one form or another,” Delanoë said, potentially combining a major surface combatant with nuclear and conventionally powered submarines and smaller missile or patrol vessels.
Until then, Russia appears to be prioritising access over permanent deployment. Tartus and Hmeimim can still facilitate military transit and links with Africa without sustaining the kind of force Moscow maintained under Assad.
This also makes Russia more dependent on governments that have their own reasons to bargain with it. For Damascus, retaining a limited Russian role provides another external relationship alongside Turkey, the Gulf states, Europe, and the United States. Russian participation in training the Syrian military could also give al-Sharaa another partner as Ankara expands its influence over Syria's security institutions.
For Moscow, meanwhile, even restricted access preserves something harder to rebuild once lost: the political and logistical infrastructure of a regional presence.
This infrastructure is political as much as military. Meenen argues that Moscow's ability to operate across this wider space depends on maintaining relationships with regional governments and avoiding disruptions along the routes connecting the Mediterranean to the Red Sea.
“Russia needs stability in the Middle East to secure its strategic interests, particularly regarding access to the Mediterranean and Red Sea,” she said.
Russia’s Syrian position is therefore unlikely to return to what it was before December 2024. Its air defence umbrella has gone, its Mediterranean squadron has disappeared, and the Syrian government now controls the terms under which Russian forces remain.
But Moscow’s wider regional strategy has not disappeared with them. It is becoming less concentrated in Syria and more dependent on a network stretching through Libya and Africa.
As Delanoë put it, Russia's future Mediterranean posture will continue to reflect “its projection of status and its claim to great-power stature,” while maintaining pressure on NATO’s southern flank and supporting relationships with countries including Algeria, Egypt and Libya.
The August agreement gives Moscow far less than it enjoyed under Assad. But after facing the possibility of losing Syria entirely, retaining Tartus and Hmeimim as part of that wider network is still a strategically useful outcome.
Francesco Salesio Schiavi is an Italian specialist in the Middle East. His focus lies in the security architecture of the Levant and the Gulf, with a particular emphasis on Iraq, Iran, and the Arab Peninsula, as well as military and diplomatic interventions by international actors
Follow him on X: @frencio_schiavi
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Ship attacked during Strait of Hormuz transit and other news from the Middle East
articles.body:
Trump says US has no talks planned with Iran and other news from the Middle East
U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday the U.S. has no talks planned with Iran but insisted the Strait of Hormuz remains “open and operating,” despite limited traffic and a reported strike on a ship exiting the waterway.
Earlier this week, Trump also threatened to bomb Oman as the country sought a deal with Iran to manage shipping traffic through the strait, two regional officials said Tuesday, a day after Trump reportedly leveled the threat if Oman “gets in the way.” Iran says the waterway will not be reopened until the U.S. meets its conditions.
As talks between Iran and Oman continue, a projectile hit a ship in the strait and Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed they fired drones at an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia.
Here’s a look at the latest developments Tuesday in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.
Trump looms over negotiations to reopen Strait of Hormuz
As Oman and Iran say they are nearing a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, Trump said on social media Tuesday that the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports remains “in full force and effect,” but asserted that all water mines have been removed and that other marine traffic was free to pass.
Trump posted a map depicting the strait as U.S. territory.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi appeared to respond to Trump’s post.
“Just as Trump correctly wrote the name of the eternal Persian Gulf, soon his delusion regarding the Strait of Hormuz will either be corrected or we will correct the delusions of this deluded man,” he wrote on X.
The Trump administration has told Oman it opposes parts of the yet-to-be-announced deal, according to officials briefed on the U.S. position. Those include joint Iranian and Omani management of the passage’s exit route and the collection of voluntary fees from vessels, even if the money is used for security and maritime environmental protection.
The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to journalists.
The White House on Tuesday referred to Trump’s remarks in the Oval Office and declined to comment further about Oman.
— By Samy Magdy in Cairo
Egypt says Iran-Oman agreement could open door to Iran-US deal
The Egyptian Foreign Ministry said Tuesday that the Iranian-Omani deal could pave the way for Washington and Tehran to return to negotiations for a “comprehensive and permanent deal that addresses all concerns and enhances regional security and stability.”
The statement came after a meeting between Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Omani counterpart Badr al-Busaidi. But it did not address Trump’s latest threat against Oman.
The 60-day negotiating period ended this week between the U.S. and Iran with no clear end to the war in sight.
Ship traffic drops significantly in Strait of Hormuz
Ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dropped significantly last week, with confirmed crossings falling 19.5% to 95 transits. Only three vessels made it through the waterway on Sunday, according to shipping data platform Kpler.
The ships used the Iranian-designated route through the strait, with no crossings recorded through the Omani routes.
Crossings through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait increased 6.7% to 254 transits, while so-called dark transits, in which ships turn off the transponders that broadcast their location, fell from 40 to 16, Kpler said.
Projectile damages ship in strait causing casualty
An unidentified projectile damaged the engine room of a ship in the Strait of Hormuz near Oman and “resulted in a crew casualty,” according to the British military’s UK Maritime Trade Operations center.
The maritime monitoring agency did not release any details about the ship or its cargo, and it was not clear whether the crew member was killed or wounded.
No environmental damage has been reported and the agency said the Omani Coast Guard was assisting other crew members and authorities were investigating.
Iran-backed Houthis claim an attack on a Saudi oil refinery
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed they fired drones at an oil refinery in neighboring Saudi Arabia, the latest attack threatening to reignite Yemen’s civil war and open another front in the Middle East.
The attack targeted a facility run by Saudi Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil company, according to a report by the Houthi-run SABA news agency. There were no immediate reports of damage or comment from Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have escalated attacks against government forces in Yemen and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government, and the kingdom’s shipping in the Red Sea, an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
Israel strike on Gaza City kills 6 people
An Israeli strike hit Gaza City on Tuesday, killing six people, including a child, and wounding 14 others, according to Shifa Hospital, where the casualties were taken.
The Israeli military said it struck Hamas commanders in the Shati area who it said were planning to carry out attacks against Israeli forces.
The heaviest fighting has subsided since a ceasefire in the more than two-year war took hold in October. Israeli forces have carried out repeated airstrikes since then, killing at least 1,266 Palestinians, according to health officials in Gaza.
The Gaza Health Ministry, which is part of the Hamas-led government, maintains detailed casualty records that are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. But it does not give a breakdown of civilians and militants.
Missiles fired at the United Arab Emirates
The defense ministry of the United Arab Emirates said two ballistic missiles were launched from Iran toward the UAE on Tuesday.
One landed outside of the country’s waters, and the other landed within them, the Emirati Defense Ministry said. It was unclear whether the missiles were shot down by air defenses or fell. No damage or injuries were reported. There was no immediate statement from Iran.
In the weeks after the U.S. and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28, the UAE was frequently targeted by Iranian missiles and drones, but Tuesday’s reported attack was the first in weeks.
Iran denies it fired missiles toward the UAE
Iran early Wednesday rejected the UAE’s claims that it launched missiles toward the country.
In a post on social media, the spokesman for the Iranian Foreign Ministry, Esmail Baghaei, said Dubai’s accusations were “detrimental to ongoing efforts to strengthen trust among the countries of the region and prevent a further deterioration of security.” He called on the nations in the region to not make “baseless accusations” against Iran.
Earlier, the UAE defense ministry said Iran launched two ballistic missiles targeting maritime traffic that fell into the sea.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Zelensky formally nominates Khmara as defense minister, rules out Fedorov's comeback
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Zelensky formally nominates Khmara as defense minister, rules out Fedorov's comeback
Key developments on Aug. 18:
- Zelensky formally taps Khmara as defense minister, ruling out Fedorov's return
- Ukraine launches hundreds of drones towards Moscow in latest large-scale attack, reportedly damaging Wildberries warehouse
- Russia threatens UK over supplying drones to Ukraine
- Ghana asks Moscow to stop recruiting its citizens for war in Ukraine
- SBU detains alleged Russian agent accused of registering Starlink terminals for Russian troops
President Volodymyr Zelensky on Aug. 18 formally nominated acting Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara, a former top Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) officer, to serve as minister in full capacity.
Zelensky also nominated Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, who served in his role in an acting capacity since the July government reshuffle, to again formally take up the post, according to lawmakers.
The decision on the new defense minister has been closely watched, as the firing of former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov during a chaotic government reshuffle sparked nationwide protests.
Both nominations must now be approved by the parliament, which returned from its summer recess on Aug. 18.
A Ukrainian official confirmed for the Kyiv Independent that Zelensky nominated Khmara and Sybiha, but noted it remains unclear when the final voting will take place. According to lawmaker Yaroslav Zhelezniak, the confirmation votes should happen on Aug. 19.
read also
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones towards Moscow in latest large-scale attack, reportedly damaging Wildberries warehouse
Ukrainian forces launched a large-scale drone attack targeting Moscow and the surrounding region overnight on Aug. 18, Russian Telegram media channels reported, citing resident accounts.
A Wildberries warehouse was reportedly damaged outside Moscow, according to Russian state media outlet Moscow 24, as Ukraine continues targeting Russia's largest online retailer.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said that at least 197 Ukrainian drones were shot down over Moscow Oblast during the attack, while Russian authorities claimed 600 had been launched at the region.
The Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channel Exilenova Plus reported that Russian air defense systems struck a residential building in the town of Pavlovsky Posad around 67 kilometers (42 miles) outside of Moscow while attempting to down the drones. A fire was seen on the roof of a building.
A fire was also reportedly seen at an aluminum plant in Moscow Oblast and a third fire was also seen burning at a home in the city of Lyubertsy, immediately outside the Moscow city boundaries.
A car and a transformer substation were damaged in the town of Elektrostal, located 58 kilometers (36 miles) east of Moscow, according to Moscow Oblast Governor Andrey Vorobyov.
OSINT analysis by independent Russian media outlet Astra also geolocated damage to the Globus shopping center in Kolomna, where parts of the facade and windows were damaged. Moscow Oblast Governor Andrey Vorobyov earlier said a nearby shopping pavilion caught fire after drone debris fell in the area.
Astra also said a drone struck one of the chimneys at the Karbolit chemical plant in Orekhovo-Zuyevo, damaging a metal maintenance platform attached to the structure. The outlet said the incident may have resulted from Russian air defense activity.
Fires were also visible in satellite imagery of the Severnoye Domodedovo warehouse complex in Moscow Oblast following the drone attack, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported. Open-source data indicates that the site houses a distribution center for the SPAR supermarket chain and was previously used by B.I. Logistics, a company specializing in the storage of radioactive materials.
read also
Russia threatens UK over supplying Ukraine with drones
Moscow on Aug. 17 issued threats against the U.K. following media reports about British drones being used in Kyiv's strikes inside Russia.
"London's actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer," the Russian Embassy to the U.K. wrote in a statement.
The Times reported on Aug. 15 that, although deep-strike missions mainly rely on Ukrainian drones, Ukraine's Armed Forces also successfully used British drones to target oil refineries near Moscow and elsewhere.
A U.K. Defense Ministry spokesperson told the Kyiv Independent that London is "committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's illegal invasion."
"Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine, and against the U.K. and our allies."
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that his government is "doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100% against this illegal war," adding that the U.K. "will be there in Ukraine's hour of need."
read also
Ghana asks Moscow to stop recruiting its citizens for war in Ukraine
Ghana has appealed to Moscow to end "illegal recruitment" of Ghanaian citizens for the Russia-Ukraine war, Ghanaian Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa said, as reported by the Russian media on Aug. 17.
According to Ablakwa, 62 of his country's citizens have been killed in Ukraine, and 15 remain missing.
The news comes amid growing concerns among governments in Africa, Asia, and elsewhere about Moscow's efforts to recruit their citizens as mercenaries for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Speaking at a press conference after talks with Ablakwa, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov alleged that Ghanaian citizens signed contracts with Russia's Defense Ministry out of "solidarity with a country that helped them fight racism," as well as for "material and financial reasons."
Ablakwa said the two ministers agreed to work together toward resolving the issue.
read also
SBU detains alleged Russian agent accused of registering 27 Starlink terminals for Moscow's troops
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) detained a suspected Russian agent in Kharkiv Oblast who allegedly registered 27 Starlink terminals in the front-line city of Izium for use by Russian forces, the agency said on Aug. 18.
According to investigators, Russian forces planned to use the equipment to coordinate assault units and drone strikes in Kharkiv Oblast.
Since February, Ukraine and SpaceX have restricted Russian access to Starlink by allowing only verified terminals to operate across Ukraine. The move diminished Russia’s ability to use the system for battlefield communications and drone operations, and helped Ukrainian counterattacks in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
To get around the restrictions, Russian forces have recruited Ukrainian citizens to register and verify Starlink terminals.
The SBU said the suspect is an unemployed displaced person from the Russian-occupied city of Khrustalnyi in Luhansk Oblast.
Investigators said Russian intelligence services recruited him after he moved to Izium and began looking for ways to earn money through Instagram.
The man allegedly first registered one Starlink terminal in his own name and passed the account details to a Russian handler based in occupied territory in eastern Ukraine.
He was later instructed to verify additional terminals and involved local residents in registering the equipment, the SBU said.
According to the agency, the suspect was also tasked with identifying the coordinates of Ukrainian military positions for Russian targeting.
The SBU said the man expected to be evacuated to Russian-occupied Luhansk Oblast after completing the assignments.

articles.title: Drills cut by Trump are central to the US-South Korea alliance
articles.body:
Drills cut by Trump are central to the US-South Korea alliance, observers say
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — For decades, the United States and South Korea have regularly staged military drills to prepare their soldiers to work together smoothly in the event of a crisis or conflict with North Korea.
But this year’s Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise, one of two main drills conducted by the allies annually, could be disrupted after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered his Pentagon chief to “substantially” scale it back just before its start Monday.
He cited what he said was a good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korea’s refusal to join the U.S. war against Iran. It was unclear what parts of the 11-day exercise were being cut and to what extent, but many experts say Trump’s move threatens to hurt combined U.S.-South Korean readiness and eventually weaken their decades-long alliance.
The exercise is central to the US-South Korea alliance
The Ulchi Freedom Shield, or UFS, is largely a computer-simulated command post exercise meant to hone the allies’ ability to deal with potential regional security threats like North Korean aggression. The two countries usually hold field training exercises during the command post exercise period.
South Korea’s military had earlier said this year’s exercise would be similar in scale to previous years, with the participation of about 18,000 South Korean soldiers. The U.S. military said it would incorporate lessons from recent conflicts such as North Korea’s battlefield experiences on the Russia-Ukraine front. Local media reported South Korea and the U.S. had planned 14 field training exercises.
The UFS, along with a similar joint war game in the spring, is a central pillar of the U.S. -South Korea alliance, which dates back to the 1950-53 Korean War. But it’s also a long-running source of tensions with North Korea, which has denounced the exercises as a rehearsal for war and responded with provocative missile tests.
On Friday, North Korea’s Foreign Ministry accused the U.S. and South Korea of plotting more provocative drills this year and vowed to respond with “a new level of a deterrent.” The U.S. and South Korea have said their regular drills are defensive in nature.
Field training will likely be affected by Trump’s decision
In a social media post, Trump called the exercise costly, “with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America.” During his first term, Trump complained about the cost of drills with South Korea, suspending joint exercises in 2018 to advance now-stalled nuclear negotiations with North Korea.
Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of about 28,500 U.S. troops stationed in South Korea, visited South Korean Defense Minister Ahn Gyu-back on Tuesday for talks likely focusing on the adjustment of this year’s drills, according to media reports. South Korea’s Defense Ministry said it couldn’t confirm the reports.
Yang Uk, an analyst at Seoul’s Asan Institute for Policy Studies, said the U.S. will likely participate in the command post exercise but cancel “some costly field training that requires large-scale movements of troops.”
Yang said that a downsizing or suspension of military drills matters because commanders of the allies change periodically. He said a one-year suspension of drills would see commanders unfamiliar with procedures of those drills taking part when they resume.
Trump’s move could strain the US-South Korea alliance
Jung Chang Wook, head of the Korea Defense Study Forum think tank in Seoul, said Trump’s move could result in the U.S. downsizing other regular drills with South Korea, posing “a big, crippling blow” to their joint operation posture.
Lee Illwoo, an expert with the Korea Defense Network, said downsizing the exercise will likely delay the planned transfer to a system in which wartime operational control would be exercised by a binational command led by a South Korean general.
Under the current system, the U.S. military would command joint forces in the event of war.
The South Korean and U.S. militaries had earlier said the exercise would be an opportunity to support preparations for the transfer. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday stressed the need to complete the transition during his term that ends in 2030.
Many South Koreans view the transition to South Korean leadership of the combined forces in wartime to be a matter of national sovereignty, but others worry that could weaken the alliance.

articles.title: Russia warns UK of “consequences” over British-made drones in Ukraine’s deep strikes. London vows to continue supporting Kyiv
articles.body:
Russia has threatened Britain with “consequences” over reports that Ukrainian forces used drones manufactured by UK companies to carry out strikes inside Russia.
The Russian Embassy in London accused the UK of deliberately escalating the war by supporting Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign, saying Britain was seeking to “contain Russia and inflict maximum damage on it by proxy.” It warned that the deeper Britain becomes involved, “the higher the price it will pay.”
The threat followed news that Ukrainian forces had used two British-built drone systems to strike targets inside Russia for the first time. The Sunday Times, citing Ukrainian military sources, reported that the drones had been used against targets including oil refineries in Volgograd and Yaroslavl over the past six months.
Moscow warns Britain of “consequences”
The Russian Embassy said in a statement that the reported use of British-made drones “confirms that London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis.”
It warned that British actions would “inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” without specifying what form those consequences could take.
The warning comes as Ukraine has significantly expanded its long-range strike campaign against Russian military and energy targets. Kyiv has increasingly used large drone swarms to hit targets deep inside Russia, seeking to disrupt military production, logistics, and energy revenues while forcing Moscow to spread its air defenses across a much larger area.
Burnham says UK will continue backing Ukraine
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham rejected Moscow’s warning, saying Britain would continue supporting Ukraine despite Russian threats, The Independent reported on Tuesday.
“This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100 per cent against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin,” Burnham said during a visit to Wolverhampton.
“We are providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself,” he said, adding: “We are not fair weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.”
UK Work and Pensions Minister Lilian Greenwood similarly said Britain’s resolve to support Ukraine remained “completely steadfast” and that the country would continue providing the military equipment Kyiv needs.
The UK Ministry of Defence also said Russia should have “no doubt” about the government's resolve to oppose Russian aggression in Ukraine and against Britain and its allies.
British drones expand Ukraine’s deep-strike capabilities
According to The Sunday Times, one of the British systems used by Ukraine is the Nyan, a jet-powered one-way attack drone produced by BAE Systems subsidiary Callen-Lenz, with a reported range of more than 150 miles.
The second system has a reported range exceeding 600 miles, although its manufacturer was not identified for security reasons. The drones provide Ukraine with additional long-range strike capacity that can be produced and deployed in larger numbers than more expensive Western cruise missiles.
British drones hit Russia for first time in Ukraine’s deep-strike campaign – The Sunday Times
The reported deployment marks a further expansion of UK military support for Ukraine as Kyiv increasingly takes the fight to Russian military and energy infrastructure inside Russia.

articles.title: Russia warns UK of ‘consequences’ over reports Ukraine using British drones in attacks
articles.body:
Andy Burnham says the UK will continue to “support Ukraine 100%” after Russia threatened consequences after strikes by British-made drones.
The Russian embassy to the UK said on Monday that Britain had been deliberately escalating the Ukraine conflict and the deeper its involvement, “the higher the price it will pay”.
Burnham, asked during a visit to Wolverhampton on Tuesday for his response to Moscow’s threat, said: “This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100% against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin.
“We are providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself, and that’s been the British position all the way through this conflict by previous prime ministers. It remains the case with me. We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.”
The use of the drones made by UK companies is part of Ukraine’s “deep strike” campaign. However, it is not the first time Ukraine has deployed British-made equipment in Russia, having long used Storm Shadow missiles.
Kyiv has stepped up its attacks this year, with long-range missiles and swarms of drones increasingly targeting Russia’s military industries and energy facilities.
It has also hit large depots of Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, burning merchandise worth billions of pounds and bringing the war home to the Russian public more than four years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russia’s embassy to the UK said on Monday that the reports confirmed that “London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis”, accusing Britain of “seeking to contain Russia and inflict maximum damage on it by proxy”.
“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” it said. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”
A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “Britain stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and we are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin’s illegal invasion. Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies.”
Ukraine’s strategy of long-range drone strikes is thought to be intended to cut Moscow’s revenue for the war and to make Russian civilians feel the impact of the invasion.
Kyiv launched three times as many such strikes in July as it did in January, according to data from Acled, an independent conflict monitor.
Repeatedly hitting deep into Russia has forced Moscow to stretch its air defences over a larger area. Russia’s defence ministry said on Saturday it had shot down 598 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions as well as the Black Sea, the Azov Sea and the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea.
Officials said on Monday that Ukrainian long-range attacks on Russia killed seven people overnight, while five civilians died in Ukraine after strikes by Moscow’s forces.
Russian missile attacks on Tuesday killed 10 people and injured eight in a village in Ukraine’s north-eastern Kharkiv oblast, the regional governor said.
The strike on the village of Pechenihy damaged 10 private buildings, a cafe, a post office, a shop and at least seven cars, Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram.
A rapid development of largely homegrown technologies, including the Flamingo cruise missile and the FP-1 long-range fixed-wing drone from Fire Point, have allowed Ukraine to bomb warehouses, oil refineries, ports and military facilities up to 1,500 miles (2,400km) from its border.
Ukraine can now almost match the deep-strike capability Russia has had since the beginning of the war using large drones and cruise missiles, though it does not possess the high-speed ballistic missiles Moscow frequently uses.
At the same time, both sides’ air defences are stretched to the point of near exhaustion, leading to an increase in civilian casualties and worries that the impact of the conflict beyond the immediate frontlines will only increase into the winter.
