articles.title: Israel kills six in Gaza on day after Kushner meeting with Netanyahu, medics say
articles.body:
Israel kills six in Gaza on day after Kushner meeting with Netanyahu, medics say
CAIRO, Aug 18 - An Israeli airstrike killed at least six Palestinians in the Gaza Strip on Tuesday, health officials said, a day after Donald Trump's envoy Jared Kushner ended a trip to the region that failed to push forward the U.S. president's plan to end the war in Gaza.
Israel's military said it had carried out an airstrike on Hamas commanders and several other militants. It said one of those targeted had taken part in the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack on Israel that triggered the war.
Gaza medics said that as well as the six dead, 14 others were wounded when the Israeli plane fired two missiles at a small cafe inside the fishing harbour in western Gaza City.
The seaport has turned into a large displacement camp for Palestinian families during the war that began in October 2023.
Blood stained the ground that was strewn with debris and people's shoes after the airstrike.
The Israeli military had initially said the strike targeted the Hamas commanders, who it said had planned to carry out attacks against Israeli troops in Gaza before later saying several other militants were also killed. It did not release evidence.
KUSHNER MEETINGS
Hamas accused Israel of trying to sabotage Trump's plan to end the war, which both Israel and Hamas agreed to last year, but said the Palestinian militant group was committed to the agreement. It said a child was among those killed in the strike.
Hamas did not say whether any of its commanders or any other militants had been killed in the strike. The militant group rarely acknowledges casualties amongst its own ranks.
Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, left Jerusalem on Monday without a breakthrough after meeting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. A day earlier, he met mediators and Hamas leaders in Egypt over ways to enhance the implementation of Trump's new roadmap for Gaza, with Hamas and Israel staying firm on their main demands.
After the meetings, an official from Trump's so-called Board of Peace, which put forward the roadmap, said Israel retained its “full right of self defence” and that there would be no “redeployment” by the Israeli military until Hamas was disarmed.
An Israeli official said Netanyahu made it clear that the military would continue to operate in Gaza and that there would be no pullback of Israeli troops.
BOTH SIDES DISPUTE SEQUENCE
In what had appeared to be a possible breakthrough at the end of last month, Trump announced that Hamas had accepted the roadmap, which said the Palestinian militant group would decommission its weapons in phases as Israel’s military withdrew from Gaza. The military would also stop its operations in the territory.
Netanyahu, whose ruling coalition is trailing ahead of an October election, rejected the roadmap, insisting that the military would only withdraw once Hamas is completely disarmed.
Hamas has demanded that Israel adhere to the ceasefire and withdraw its forces from Gaza. Both sides have disputed the sequencing of how Trump's plan should be implemented.
“If they (Hamas) don't follow through now on their commitment, everyone will see that they're not genuine about peace, and then Israel will have a lot more support from the U.S. and others to go and finish the job in the appropriate way," Kushner told Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst in an interview on Monday.
More than 1,200 Palestinians and four Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since a ceasefire was reached in October, according to Gazan health officials and the Israeli military. REUTERS

articles.title: Zelenskyy Nominates Defense Chief, Russian Missiles Kill 10, Drone Hits Nuclear Plant Workers
articles.body:
A popular former defense minister whose dismissal last month sparked protests has delivered a videotaped address to Ukrainians in which he assailed wartime corruption, warned of a systemic crisis of governance, and said the country must find a way to hold elections despite the continuing Russian invasion.
Mykhaylo Fedorov's remarks late on August 18 came hours after lawmakers said President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who abruptly pushed him out in mid-July, has asked parliament to confirm acting Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara in the role. A vote is expected on August 19.
His comments could add to pressure on Zelenskyy, who has substantial public support but has been dogged by corruption scandals and questions over the motives of a rash of recent personnel decisions. Supporters have held protests since Fedorov's dismissal.
Zelenskyy was elected to a five-year term in 2019, but martial law in place since Russia launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 means no elections have been held.
"Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia. We are fighting precisely because we want to remain a free European state. Therefore, we must find a legal, safe and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to restore a full-fledged democratic process even in the conditions of a protracted war," Fedorov said.
"This is difficult," he went on. "We need to ensure the right to vote for the military, millions of Ukrainians abroad, and people in front-line regions. We need to ensure the security of the electoral process, the independence of institutions, and trust in the result."
Wartime corruption is not just a financial problem but a question of "the ability to survive and win," he said, declaring a systemic crisis of governance in Ukraine.
In what seemed like a criticism of Zelenskyy, he said Ukrainians have always given their government a major credit of trust, especially during the war, and that this is "a huge responsibility for any government. Because a credit of trust is not the right to do everything without explanation. It is an obligation to be even more honest with society."
"This is where the simple principle of a new social contract should exist: a citizen trusts the state -- the state speaks honestly with the citizen," Fedorov said.
Zelenskyy dismissed Fedorov amid a dispute between the tech-savvy defense chief who had been in the job for just six months, and the top military commander, General Oleksandr Syrskiy, who was himself dismissed by the president days later after more than two years in the role.
Lawmakers in the Verkhovna Rada, Ukraine's parliament, said on August 18 that Zelenskyy had submitted his nomination of Khmara, a major general who had been acting chief of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) since January.
A vote is expected on the nomination of Khmara and the renomination of Andriy Sybiha, who has been foreign minister since September 2024. That is a necessary step because Zelenskyy triggered the full cabinet's resignation when he pushed Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko out on July 12; she was replaced by Serhiy Koretskiy.
The shakeups come as Ukraine fights to defend itself against Russia's full-scale invasion while facing a glaring shortage of air-defense missiles, due in part to a decline in supplies of US-made Patriot systems since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in February.
Russian missiles fired overnight damaged private homes, a cafe, a post office, a shop and several cars in the town of Pechenihiy in the eastern Kharkiv region, killing 10 people and injuring eight others, the head of the regional military administration, Oleh Synyehubov, said on Telegram.
Later on August 18, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said it was told by the director of Ukraine's Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhya nuclear power plant, that a drone hit a bus stop used by plant staff and subcontractors at about 6 a.m., killing one person and injuring 15 others, three of them seriously.
"No nuclear safety or security damage was reported," the IAEA said in a post on X.
IAEA chief Rafael Grossi "calls on military commanders responsible for these actions as well as all others aiming on nuclear power plants and/or their staff to put an immediate stop to these unacceptable actions which...constitute great risks to nuclear safety and security during the conflict," the post said.
Russia blamed Ukraine for the drone hit. There was no immediate comment from Kyiv.
The Zaporizhzhya plant is Europe's largest nuclear power station, with six reactors. Russian forces seized it shortly after Moscow launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and Ukraine and Russia have traded accusations of shelling and other actions threatening the safety of the plant, which lies across the Dnieper River from Ukrainian-held territory.
A Russian drone hit a combine harvester at a separate location in the Zaporizhzhya region on August 18, killing one farm worker and injuring another, Ukrainian officials said.

articles.title: Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,210 Troops, 5 Air Defense Systems, and 55 Artillery Systems
articles.body:

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,210 Troops, 5 Air Defense Systems, and 55 Artillery Systems
Russian forces lost an estimated 1,210 troops, two tanks, and five air defense systems over the past 24 hours, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on August 18.
The latest figures bring Russia’s total estimated personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, to approximately 1,469,970.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff, Russian forces also lost seven armored combat vehicles, 55 artillery systems, three multiple launch rocket systems, 19 UGVs, and 1,962 operational-tactical UAVs during the reporting period.
Ukraine additionally reported the destruction of 443 vehicles and fuel tankers and seven pieces of special equipment.
Russia’s cumulative equipment losses are now estimated at 12,274 tanks, 25,162 armored combat vehicles, 48,155 artillery systems, 2,040 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,577 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 2,292 UGVs, 467,459 operational-tactical UAVs, 5,010 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, two submarines, 135,891 vehicles and fuel tankers, and 4,547 pieces of special equipment.
Ukraine’s General Staff recorded 244 combat engagements between Ukrainian and Russian forces across the front over the past 24 hours.
Earlier, the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine reported that Ukraine’s Armed Forces are inflicting losses on Russia worth several times more than the cost of the weapons used to cause them.

articles.title: Iran's drone strike on Kurds may be warning over Trump administration's backchannel, analyst says
articles.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the drone attack on the office of the Kurdistan Democratic Party leader, posting on X/Twitter on Monday that “Kurdish friends” should be aware of “false-flag ploys” aimed at “sowing discord between neighbors.”
Two drones targeted the office of Masrour Barzani, the Kurdistan Regional Government’s (KRG) prime minister, and the home of the region’s intelligence chief in northern Iraq on Monday, the KRG security agency announced.
The attack was launched from Iranian territory, it said in a statement
“Nothing justifies the reckless attack on PM Barzani’s office. Kurdish friends should be vigilant against false-flag ploys to sow discord between neighbors,” Araghchi wrote. “We protected our Kurdish friends against Saddam [Hussein] and Daesh (ISIS), and we’re thankful for the security they’ve provided on our border.”
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei doubled down on Araghchi’s statements in comments to Iranian state media on Monday, describing the attack as “highly suspicious.”
“This development is highly suspicious and requires all sides to exercise vigilance,” he told IRNA, adding that he had information indicating that Iraqi intelligence was holding groups responsible for planning and carrying out the “sinister plots.”
Security analyst accuses Iran's response of being incomplete
Security analyst Roger Macmillan said that the response by the Iranian officials was lacking.
“The Kurdistan Counter-Terrorism Service didn’t just say ‘Iran did this.’ They named the munition type, two Hadid-110 drones, and stated a launch origin inside Iranian territory,” he explained.
“That’s a forensic claim, not a political one. A false-flag narrative needs to explain how a third party sourced and launched an Iranian-designated drone type from inside Iran’s own territory. Araghchi’s statement doesn’t engage with that detail at all; it simply asserts the incident is ‘suspicious’ and pivots to blaming unnamed others.”
The attack came after a report from Axios published on Sunday claimed that the Trump administration used Iraqi Kurdistan President Nechirvan Barzani as a back channel to speak with the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Commander Ahmad Vahidi. A spokesperson later confirmed the report to Iran International.
Macmillan said that the fact that the strike came within days of the confirmation indicated that the motive behind the attack was to punish KRG and warn its leadership against making further admissions going forward.
IRGC attacks Kurdish territories, 'Post' confirms
Erbil has seen frequent attacks from Iran since the outbreak of the war. A Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan (PDKI) report seen by The Jerusalem Post claimed that between February 28 and August 1, the IRGC and affiliated groups were responsible for 423 attacks on five Kurdish organizations in the territory, resulting in 20 casualties. The Post has also previously spoken with Ardalan Mama, whose home was destroyed by an Iranian missile.
Since the outbreak of the war, Araghchi has frequently commented on the risk of alleged false-flag attacks. In March, he warned his Turkish counterpart of repeated false-flag operations aimed at undermining regional ties a day after NATO intercepted a ballistic missile fired from Iran over Turkey, and only weeks ago he described a drone strike on Egypt’s Damietta Port as an Israeli false-flag operation.
“Egypt is considered a friend and important partner in the region, and its security constitutes an utmost priority for us. We must all remain vigilant toward Israeli schemes and “false flag” operations that aim to undermine regional peace,” he wrote. “The threat is clear, shared, and fears Muslim solidarity.”

articles.title: Moscow says Britain will ‘have to answer’ for the UK-made drones hitting Russian refineries
articles.body:
Moscow says Britain will ‘have to answer’ for the UK-made drones hitting Russian refineries
The Russian Embassy in London has accused the United Kingdom of “deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis” after news reports said British-made drones had been used in strikes deep inside Russia.
“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” the embassy said in a statement. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv’s terrorist machine, the higher the price it will pay for this.”
The embassy did not specify exactly what “consequences” the United Kingdom should expect. Russia has threatened Britain before over British deliveries of Storm Shadow missiles and drone-manufacturing technology to Ukraine.
Britain’s Defense Ministry told the BBC that the country stands “shoulder to shoulder” with Ukraine. “We are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin’s illegal invasion,” a ministry representative said.
On August 16, The Sunday Times first reported the use of British drones in long-range strikes. According to the newspaper, Ukraine has recently received two types of drones from the United Kingdom: one with a range of about 150 miles (240 kilometers), the other about 600 miles (960 kilometers).
The newspaper said the drones were used in this summer’s campaign of long-range strikes on Russian territory, including attacks on oil refineries and warehouses belonging to the Russian online retailer Wildberries. A well-placed military source later confirmed to the BBC that British drones had been used.
Britain’s Defense Ministry first said in April that it would send long-range strike drones to Ukraine, as part of an aid package worth 500 million pounds — the largest such package since the start of the war. The package reportedly included more than 150,000 drones.
The war in photos: Pechenihy, Ukraine’s Kharkiv region
Russian forces carried out a missile strike on the village of Pechenihy in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region on Tuesday morning, hitting a crowded intersection where a post office, stores, and homes stand. Ukrainian authorities said 10 people were killed and 17 injured. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine “will certainly respond to this Russian strike.”

articles.title: Ukraine, Russia trade strikes; Wildberries site hit again
articles.body:
Ukraine, Russia trade strikes; Wildberries site hit again
August 18, 2026
Ukraine and Russia traded more attacks overnight, with the Kharkiv regional governor reporting 10 dead civilians not far from the Russian border and the Moscow mayor saying Ukraine launched some 620 drones toward the region.
This follows one of the largest Ukrainian attacks on Russia during the war over the weekend, and the UN warning that amplified Russian strikes on towns and cities in July meant that civilian deaths in the conflict rose to levels not seen since May 2022 and the earliest months of combat.
The drone attacks on the Moscow area again caused minor damage at a facility belonging to Russian online retail giant Wildberries, a frequent target for Ukrainian forces of late.
What happened in the Kharkiv missile strike?
The governor of the Kharkiv oblast, Oleh Syniehubov, on Tuesday said that the 10 people were killed and 18 more wounded in a Russian missile strike on the village of Pechenihy.
"The strike damaged 10 private houses, a cafe, a post office, a shop and at least seven cars," Syniehubov wrote on Telegram, noting that the casualty figures were preliminary.
He said emergency services were responding and dealing with the attack.
Parts of the Kharkiv region in northeastern Ukraine are occupied by Russian forces. Both Kharkiv and the Belgorod region across the border in Russia have been targeted frequently throughout the war.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack targeted a busy intersection.
What happened as hundreds of drones approached Moscow?
Moscow's Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Tuesday that some 620 drones had flown towards the capital region overnight. He said that most were intercepted on approach, and another 180 were shot down over the Moscow area.
Russian state news agency TASS called it the heaviest such attack in two years. Russia's Defense Ministry said that, in total, it repelled 791 Ukrainian drones overnight across Russian territoy and the annexed Crimean Peninsula. The figures cannot be verified but indicate the intensity of Ukrainian strikes into Russian territory in recent days.
Moscow's regional governor, Andrei Vorobyov, issued more details on the damage caused by the drones shot down over the capital, giving a slightly lower figure of "over 150."
He said that three people were injured in three separate districts, including a young girl with a shrapnel wound to the hand.
Vorobyov also reported damage to several mainly residential buildings, including one house that "burned down completely in the village of Kuznetsy."
He said that a drone also struck a "Wildberries warehouse near Atlant-Park" in the city of Kolomna, which also logged damage at a retail site near a shopping center.
What did Russia say about reports of UK drones being used in strikes on its territory?
Russia's Embassy in London also turned its attention to drone attacks this week, responding critically on Monday evening to reports in newspaper The Times saying that drones supplied by the UK had been used in attacks on Russian territory.
The embassy asserted that such reports "confirm that London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis, while hypocritically professing a desire for peace."
It accused the UK of "acting as an accomplice and co-perpetrator of the bloody crimes and terrorist attacks committed by Ukrainian neo-Nazis," and said that "London's actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer."
What did Germany's environment minister say during his visit to Kyiv?
Also on Tuesday, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider traveled to Kyiv.
The Social Democrat (SPD) politician planned to spend several days in the country this week if circumstances allow.
"The goal of the trip is to work with our Ukrainian partners to identify, at an early stage, opportunities for a climate-friendly, resilient renewal of infrastructure and further reconstruction, including with the participation of the German business community," the Envirnoment Ministry said on Tuesday as Schneider was arriving.
The minister was accompanied by business representatives, not least from companies specializing in climate-friendly technologies.
Schneider also planned to be briefed on the situation for Ukraine's nuclear power plants, including the damage to protective dome covering the Chernobyl or Chornobyl reactor that melted down in the 1980s during the Soviet era.
"Its repair is highly complex," the ministry said.
Ukraine's main functioning nuclear power plant at Zaporizhzhia, meanwhile, has been under Russian military occupation and operational control since the first weeks of the war in 2022. Its reactors are in cold shutdown status but the plant still requires external power, cooling and maitenance. Close to the front lines, the plant and the surrounding area has fairly frequently come under fire.
Edited by: Louis Oelofse

articles.title: US Awards Raytheon $22.9 Billion Deal to Boost Tomahawk
articles.body:
The US military awarded Raytheon, an RTX unit, a $22.9 billion contract to sharply increase Tomahawk missile production as Washington seeks to replenish depleted stocks of high-tech weapons, according to Reuters.
As established on Monday, the seven-year contract will allow Raytheon to increase annual Tomahawk production from its current 60 missiles to more than 1,000.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The agreement formalizes a framework deal signed between the US military and Raytheon in February and is part of the Trump administration’s broader effort to expand the US defense industrial base.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions during the Iran conflict, raising concerns over inventories of air defense and precision-guided weapons.
Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said the contract would help ensure the US military maintains sufficient missile supplies.
“We called on industry to rapidly scale up munitions output, and RTX is delivering,” Cao said in a post on X. “This landmark Tomahawk contract ensures our warfighters continue to have the lethal firepower they need.”
The sea-launched Tomahawk is a long-range precision-strike missile used by the US Navy against land targets from ships and submarines.
US pushes broader weapons production
The Raytheon contract is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to secure multi-year agreements with major US defense contractors. The longer contracts are intended to give companies greater confidence to invest in new manufacturing facilities and equipment.
Baker Tilly to Audit Ukraine’s Defense Procurement Agency After Stormy Year of Disputes
Earlier in August, the US military also signed agreements aimed at increasing production of components for Patriot and THAAD interceptor missiles.
Previously, President Donald Trump said that major US automakers General Motors and Ford would also become involved in expanding weapons production, including Patriot air defense and Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said the companies were discussing ways to repurpose idle factory capacity for defense manufacturing.
“We are building a lot of factories across the country,” Trump said, adding that General Motors was “very interested” in the initiative and could reopen several plants.
The move follows concerns over US missile stockpiles and comes as Washington seeks to use more commercial manufacturing capacity to accelerate weapons production.

articles.title: Russian Jet-Powered ‘Shahed’ Drone Reaches Western Ukraine for First Time
articles.body:
A Russian jet-powered “Shahed” drone flew approximately 900 kilometers (nearly 560 miles) from its launch point in Crimea into western Ukraine on Tuesday, Aug. 18, marking the farthest such strike recorded so far.
According to the eRadar monitoring channel, which conducted a detailed analysis of the drone’s flight, the drone traveled from Crimea through Mykolaiv, Vinnytsia, and Khmelnytskyi regions before passing near Kremenets in the Ternopil region and eventually reaching the city of Dubno in the Rivne region.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The drone covered a distance of 850 to 920 kilometers (roughly 528 to 572 miles) when accounting for maneuvering, with a straight-line penetration depth of more than 720 kilometers (about 447 miles) from its launch point.
“Today’s tracked route of an enemy jet-powered drone is a clear demonstration of how the enemy is testing our air defense system and searching for new corridors using jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs),” eRadar said.
A route built to avoid air defenses
The drone’s transit through southern, central, and western Ukraine indicates the route “was calculated in advance to avoid the main deployment areas” of Ukraine’s anti-aircraft missile systems, eRadar said.
The monitoring group described this as evidence that Russia is actively searching for “blind spots” in the country’s air defense network, rather than flying a direct line toward a fixed target.
Stun Grenade Injures 4 in Russian School After Counter-Terrorism Exercise Goes Wrong
According to RBC-Ukraine, citing Rivne Regional Military Administration head Oleksandr Koval, an aerial target – likely the same type of jet-powered drone – was shot down over the southern part of the region.
The interception came after Ukraine’s Air Force tracked the drone crossing multiple regions over the course of roughly 30 minutes.
Speed complicating ground defense
The drone’s jet engine, which reaches speeds of 400 to 600 kilometers per hour (roughly 249 to 373 miles per hour), significantly reduces the chances of interception, particularly using small arms or large-caliber machine guns.
“Therefore, ‘classic’ mobile fire groups are completely impractical in this case,” eRadar said.
Until now, jet-powered drones had a typical operational range of up to 500 kilometers (around 310 miles), which limited their use largely to regions such as Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa, Sumy, Poltava, Dnipropetrovsk, and the Chernihiv region, RBC-Ukraine reported.
Tuesday’s flight nearly doubled that distance, suggesting Russia has modified its drone models to extend their range.
Broader implications
The extended range means that “virtually the entire territory of Ukraine – right up to its most remote western borders” now falls within the zone of possible Russian strikes, eRadar said.
According to a separate report from the Institute for the Study of War on Monday, Aug. 17, Russia is expanding its network of drone launch sites, with western Ukraine emerging as a likely future target.
Speaking on Monday, Anton Zemlyanyi, a senior analyst at the Ukrainian Center for Security and Cooperation said Russia is increasingly relying on faster drones as the effectiveness of conventional Shaheds in large-scale attacks declines.

articles.title: Two Russian missiles hit a post office and shops in Kharkiv Oblast, killing 10 people
articles.body:
Russia struck the center of Pechenihy, a settlement in Ukraine's Kharkiv Oblast, on the morning of 18 August, killing at least 10 people and wounding at least 18, Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported. Two missiles hit a post office and shops at a crossroads ringed by homes, setting a cafe and cars ablaze. Emergency crews recovered bodies from the rubble as rescue work continued through the day.
A strike at rush hour
Russia fired two Banderol cruise missiles into the settlement at 08:40, the Prosecutor General's Office said, opening a war-crimes investigation into the deaths. The missiles hit the central part of Pechenihy just as residents were heading to work and businesses were opening, the settlement's head, Oleksandr Husarov, said. He put the preliminary midday toll as high as 20 wounded, cautioning the figures were not final.
Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Oblast Military Administration, reported that the strike burned a cafe and seven cars across roughly 400 m², and damaged 10 private houses, the post office, five shops, and 15 vehicles.
The Banderol is a low-cost, jet-powered cruise missile that Russia has used against Ukrainian cities before. Built by the sanctioned firm Kronshtadt with foreign components, it reaches up to 650 km/h and carries a 114.3-kg warhead. Ukraine recently found that a new ground launcher could let Russia fire the missile in salvos and without warning.
Ukraine's response
Acting Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Putin "continues to drag out the war instead of accepting Ukraine's realistic ceasefire proposals." President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had "brutally struck a crowded crossroads" where the post office and shops stood, ringed only by homes, and vowed a response, urging partners to add pressure on Moscow.
The same day, Russia also struck the Kharkiv Oblast city of Izium, wounding five people, among them a nine-year-old child, and damaging five private houses, Syniehubov said. Emergency services worked at the site and the wounded received care.

articles.title: UN watchdog excavates suspected Syrian nuclear site as Damascus pledges safeguards
articles.body:
UN watchdog excavates suspected Syrian nuclear site as Damascus pledges safeguards
DAMASCUS, Syria (AP) — Inspectors with the United Nations’ nuclear watchdog have begun excavating at a site believed to be linked to a clandestine nuclear program run by Syria’s former government, the agency’s chief said on Thursday.
The announcement came as Syria’s new government has pledged to cooperate with the watchdog. Syria’s top diplomat said Thursday that Damascus remains interested in developing a peaceful nuclear program and intends to keep any nuclear material in its custody under international safeguards.
Under former President Bashar Assad, Syria was believed to have operated an extensive undeclared nuclear program that included a nuclear reactor built by North Korea in eastern Deir el-Zour province.
Syria under Assad allowed IAEA inspectors to visit some sites, but the country under interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa has pledged full cooperation with the UN watchdog and given its inspectors access to suspected nuclear sites.
“Myself and my team, we were inside the site of Deir el-Zour, where very comprehensive work of excavation and exploration is taking place now,” the International Atomic Energy Agency’s director-general Rafael Mariano Grossi said at a news conference in Damascus.
Grossi said another site with nuclear material has also been discovered, but did not disclose any details.
Grossi said Syria’s cooperation has “enormous importance.”
“We’re talking about a few tons of nuclear material that could be put to bad use and Syria has decided to open up this site to the inspectors of the IAEA,” Grossi said. “This material will be accounted for and will be put within the international safeguard system.”
Syria under its new leadership has expressed an intention to develop nuclear energy.
“Syria confirms, based on technical evaluations, that this material does not pose any danger,” Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani said. “It will remain in Syria’s custody and will remain subject to the agency’s safeguard system.”
The site in Deir el-Zour only became public knowledge after Israel launched airstrikes in 2007 that destroyed the facility. Syria later leveled the site and never responded fully to the IAEA’s questions about it.
However, in 2024, before Assad was deposed in December of that year, IAEA inspectors took samples at three locations and in 2025 said they had found traces of uranium at one site.
Israel is believed to be the Middle East’s only state with nuclear weapons, although it has not declared its own program.
___
Chehayeb reported from Beirut. Associated Press producer Malak Harb in Beirut contributed to this report.

articles.title: Report: US weighs shrinking military footprint in Middle East after Iran batters bases
articles.body:
The Pentagon is reassessing the scale of the U.S. military presence in the Middle East, including whether to reduce forces stationed in the Gulf after months of Iranian attacks damaged American bases across the region, The Washington Post reported Tuesday.
The report, based on eight officials and people familiar with the discussions, said the destruction created what some Pentagon officials view as a “once-in-a-generation opportunity” to reconsider how the United States deploys forces in the region rather than simply rebuilding damaged installations as they existed before the war.
One Pentagon official said the Joint Chiefs of Staff and U.S. Central Command are examining the issue. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has not yet ordered a formal force posture review, the official said, describing the current effort instead as “prudent planning” that could later help the administration decide whether and how to reconstruct bases damaged during the fighting.
One proposal under discussion would reportedly involve moving some forces to Israel, but the idea has generated disagreement in Washington because of concerns about Israeli espionage, according to the report.
The broader debate comes as the Gulf remains under threat. The United Arab Emirates activated missile warnings earlier Tuesday after authorities said they detected a missile threat directed at the country.
Alerts sounded in Dubai for the first time in about six weeks, while residents received warnings on their phones instructing them to remain in safe locations and follow official guidance. About half an hour later, the UAE Interior Ministry announced that “the situation is safe.”
The Emirati Defense Ministry said its forces remained fully prepared to respond to threats and protect the country’s sovereignty, security and stability.
The renewed alert underscored the continuing volatility facing Gulf states even as Washington considers whether its traditional military footprint in the region remains sustainable.
Earlier Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump posted what he presented as an annexation map of the Strait of Hormuz on Truth Social after previously threatening to declare the strategic waterway American territory.
Trump later wrote that no talks with Iran were underway or scheduled, adding that the U.S. naval blockade remained fully in force and that the Strait of Hormuz was “open and operating.”
“There are no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled, with the Islamic Republic of Iran. The Naval Blockade remains in full force and effect. The Hormuz Strait is open and operating. All water mines have been removed or detonated,” Trump said.
His statement contradicted remarks by his son-in-law and special envoy Jared Kushner, who had described contacts between the administration and elements of the Iranian regime as the “best ever.”
Iranian officials and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps sharply rejected Kushner’s characterization, accusing Trump of promoting a fantasy born of what they described as defeat and desperation in the war.
The Wall Street Journal reported about two weeks ago that the UAE had pressed Trump to launch a broad attack on Iran, while Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan urged him not to do so.
Trump was reported to have seriously considered strikes on Iranian facilities and infrastructure before ultimately deciding against them.
Israeli assessments have warned that Tehran could seek to widen the regional confrontation if it concludes that the continuing naval blockade threatens regime stability. Recent reports have suggested that Iranian officials increasingly view the confrontation as extending well beyond the battlefield.
The blockade and the disruption of Iran’s ability to export oil and generate revenue are adding economic pressure on the regime as Washington continues to use financial leverage alongside military pressure.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran had decided to shift its posture from defensive to “fully offensive.”
“All Iranian bodies will be prepared for an escalation of tensions in the Strait of Hormuz and in the region if diplomatic efforts fail,” the official said.
The same official claimed Iran had given the United States several weeks to fully implement the memorandum of understanding reached between the sides.
Against that backdrop, the Pentagon’s reassessment reflects a larger strategic question for Washington: whether the heavy damage inflicted on longstanding U.S. bases should be treated as a reason to restore the old military architecture of the Gulf, or as an opportunity to build a smaller and potentially different American presence in the region.

articles.title: Russia threatens Britain over Ukraine’s use of UK drones
articles.body:
Russia has threatened Britain with consequences after reports confirmed that Ukraine used British-made drones to strike targets inside Russia. Moscow accused London of escalating the war, while the British government said it would continue supplying Kyiv with military equipment.
Russia’s embassy in London said Britain had “deliberately” chosen escalation by providing equipment used against targets on Russian territory.
“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” the embassy said. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”
The warning followed reporting by The Sunday Times that Ukraine had used drones produced by two British companies in attacks on Russian military and industrial sites. A military source later confirmed the use of UK-made drones to the BBC.
The Sunday Times identified one system as the Nyan drone produced by Callen-Lenz, a subsidiary of defence group BAE Systems. The newspaper withheld the identity of the second manufacturer for security reasons.
According to the newspaper, the second drone has a range approaching 1,000 kilometres. The Nyan has a reported range of about 240 kilometres.
Ukraine has expanded long-range attacks against Russian oil refineries, military facilities and logistics centres. Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, has also suffered strikes on its warehouses.
Ukraine says seven of the company’s 10 largest logistics centres have been disabled. The Sunday Times estimated damage linked to attacks involving British drones at more than €40 billion. The BBC cited a military source who put economic damage at more than £35 billion.
A Wildberries warehouse near Moscow was struck during another wave of attacks this week. Regional governor Andrey Vorobyov said firefighters extinguished a fire at the facility. Wildberries described the damage as minor.
Russian officials said about 620 drones headed towards the Moscow region overnight from Monday into Tuesday. Air defences intercepted more than 180.
Ukraine has also faced another series of Russian attacks. Zaporizhzhia regional governor Ivan Fedorov said two people were killed and four injured after Russia launched 1,158 strikes against 59 settlements in the region over 24 hours.
In the Kharkiv region, a Russian missile strike on Pechenihy killed 10 people and injured eight on Tuesday, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram.
Britain rejected Moscow’s warning.
“Britain stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and we are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin’s illegal invasion,” a Ministry of Defence spokesperson said.
Britain announced in June that it would provide 150,000 drones to Ukraine by the end of 2026 under a £752 million military support package.
Russia has issued repeated warnings to Britain and other countries supplying Ukraine since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Russia now controls about a fifth of Ukrainian territory.
HT

articles.title: AI-assisted tool helped secure satellite communication system after 2022 Russian hacking
articles.body:
AI-assisted tool helped secure satellite communication system after 2022 Russian hacking
WASHINGTON (AP) — On the same day it invaded Ukraine in 2022, Russia disabled thousands of satellite modems across Ukraine and other European countries, aiming to disrupt communications. A new AI-assisted tool aims to help close that kind of vulnerability amid concerns about continued Russian aggression and newer Iranian threats to cyber infrastructure.
The cybersecurity company Atalanta has released “Argo” — a product that includes the technology that was instrumental in securing Viasat’s satellite communications network after the Russian hacking attack. Industry experts say it presents a new capability for those trying to defend critical systems in the emerging cyberwarfare theater.
Atalanta’s leaders say the new technology relies on what it calls “software understanding,” combining complex mathematics along with artificial intelligence technology to create the first commercially available system that can analyze software and internet-connected systems for vulnerabilities in a more comprehensive manner.
The conflicts in both Ukraine and Iran have highlighted the danger that hackers can pose to everyday life. This summer several government agencies have warned that Iranian hackers have been targeting water and wastewater systems, among other critical infrastructure.
“The tools and techniques of yesterday do not scale for today and ‘software understanding’ is going to be the path forward for anyone building a system of consequence for the United States,” Atalanta CEO and co-founder Anjana Rajan told The Associated Press.
Viasat’s chief of cyber strategy, Nick Saunders, said the new technology not only ensures that the Viasat network is hardened against future attacks but produces the math that backs up that claim.
“We have built over the past year, working with Atalanta ... a capability where we can start to develop an understanding of how our systems are more resilient against attacks,” Saunders said.
Atalanta’s technology has also been tapped to work on the Genesis Mission — the Department of Energy’s effort to create autonomous nuclear reactors.
Greg Shannon, the chief cybersecurity scientist at the government’s Idaho National Laboratory, said the kind of technology that Atalanta is making available will likely eventually become the standard for testing any new capability.
“In a decade or two, I would expect it to be just part of the standard development tool kits,” Shannon added.
Shannon noted that the Defense Advanced Research Project Agency, or DARPA, has been investing billions in this technology for a couple of decades. This investment helped create the demand for a system like Argo.
DARPA is the military’s cutting-edge research office, which also helped pioneer technologies such as the internet and stealth aircraft.
“They’ve probably invested well over $2 billion in various programs to advance formal methods ... and we’re finally seeing them start to come to fruition,” Shannon said.
Last year, Emil Michael, the Pentagon’s chief technology officer, told a DARPA software conference in a prerecorded address that he saw the mathematics underpinning Atalanta’s technology as the future of the military and he wanted it to “become the DoD’s gold standard” for cybersecurity.

articles.title: US voices 'deep concern' after Israel strikes Syrian airbase
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US rebukes Israel over Syria strikes after Turkish military visit
Israeli warplanes struck a military airport in northwestern Syria early on Tuesday, hours after a Turkish military delegation visited the site to begin preparations to rehabilitate its runways, in an attack that appeared to send a message to Ankara over its role in rebuilding Syria's military capabilities.
The strikes on Abu al-Duhur military airport, in the eastern countryside of Syria's Idlib province, drew condemnation from Damascus and a rare public rebuke from Washington, with US special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack describing the attack as an "unnecessary escalation" that did not serve regional stability.
The attack marked the first on the site since the fall of the Assad regime and the first Israeli airstrike in Syria since March.
A source in the Syrian Ministry of Defence told The New Arab that Israeli aircraft carried out the attack. Israel has not claimed responsibility.
The source said two strikes hit the airport's runway at around 2:50 AM local time, causing damage but no injuries or fatalities.
Syrian state-run Al-Ekhbariya, citing a military source, reported that warplanes carried out a total of eight strikes on the airport, damaging its runways. Al Jazeera separately reported four strikes on the runway.
Abu al-Duhur is the second-largest military airport in northern Syria. The sprawling facility covers around eight square kilometres and has 22 runways.
The timing of the attack, coming just hours after Turkish military officials inspected the site, has raised questions over whether Israel was seeking to warn Ankara against helping Syria rebuild its air force.
Informed sources told The New Arab that a Turkish military delegation had visited the airport on Monday as part of initial plans to rehabilitate its runways, stressing that the project remained in its early stages.
Several Turkish vehicles were still on the airport premises at the time, the sources said, while a reconnaissance aircraft was also operating in the area.
Following the Turkish delegation's visit on Monday, an Israeli reconnaissance aircraft flew over the military airport later that evening and into the early hours of Tuesday, according to the sources. The strikes followed around dawn.
The sequence suggests Israel had been closely monitoring activity at the airport ahead of the attack, with the timing pointing to a possible message to Turkey as Ankara moves to assist Syria in rebuilding its military and air capabilities.
US voices 'deep concern' over Israeli strikes
In Washington's first reaction to the attack, US special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack expressed "deep concern" over the confirmed Israeli airstrikes on Abu al-Duhur, calling them an "unnecessary escalation" that did not serve regional stability.
Barrack pointed to the approach taken by the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, saying Damascus "has not adopted a hostile posture nor maintained proxy forces, but has repeatedly demonstrated a preference for de-escalation with Israel".
He also emphasised Washington's efforts to reduce tensions between the two countries.
The United States, Barrack said, "has in the past, and will continue in the future, to host discussions to encourage a diplomatic rhythm rather than military frustration for both countries".
Sustainable de-escalation agreements, he added, are built through continued dialogue with all relevant states and actors, saying Washington continues to believe that "restraint and engagement represent the most constructive path".
Barrack called on all sides to prioritise "reasoned dialogue" over further military incidents.
His comments came as Damascus issued its own sharply worded condemnation, describing the Israeli attack as an "unjustified aggression" and a flagrant violation of Syrian sovereignty.
Syria's Foreign Ministry said the strikes represented "a dangerous escalation that threatens security and stability in the region".
It said the continued Israeli attacks since the fall of Bashar al-Assad on 8 December 2024 were taking place despite Syria exercising restraint and seeking to consolidate stability and avoid escalation.
The ministry accused Israel of attempting to undermine those efforts and "drag the region towards further tension and instability".
Damascus called on the international community and UN Security Council to clearly condemn the attack and take a "firm position towards repeated Israeli violations of Syrian sovereignty".
Syria, it added, would continue to defend its rights and national interests through legitimate means permitted under international law.
During Syria's civil war, opposition forces captured Abu al-Duhur in September 2015. The Assad regime regained control of the airport in 2018 and held it until Bashar al-Assad was ousted in December 2024.
Israel targets Syria's military capabilities
Since the fall of the Assad regime, Israel has stepped up its raids and incursions into Syria, while targeting much of the country's remaining military infrastructure.
Israeli attacks have struck Syrian air-defence systems, long- and medium-range missiles, weapons and missile depots, scientific research centres and other military facilities.
Israeli strikes have also hit several key Syrian airfields and military installations, including Hama airport, as well as Tiyas, Shayrat, Palmyra, Dumayr and Mezzeh airfields.
Syria's naval fleets at the ports of Latakia and Tartus have also been targeted, even as the country's new authorities have begun taking steps to rebuild the military and its air capabilities.
Last month, Syrian state media reported that Israeli forces had carried out a fresh incursion into southern Syria, despite a visiting UN chief demanding an end to Israeli violations.
The Syrian state news agency SANA said Israeli soldiers, accompanied by three military vehicles and a bulldozer, had established a checkpoint in al-Aarada. Israeli forces also dropped leaflets in nearby towns warning residents against closing roads.
The strikes on Abu al-Duhur mark the first time the airport has been targeted since the fall of the Assad regime.

articles.title: Britain brushes off threats from Russia
articles.body:
The Russian embassy in London has warned that Britain will pay a price for supplying drones reportedly used by Ukraine to strike targets inside Russia, in a statement accusing the UK of deliberately escalating the war.
The embassy said reports that Ukraine is using British drones for strikes deep inside Russian territory “confirm that London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis, while hypocritically professing a desire for peace.”
It said: “In doing so, the United Kingdom is acting as an accomplice and co-perpetrator of the bloody crimes and terrorist attacks committed by Ukrainian neo-Nazis, seeking to contain Russia and inflict maximum damage on it by proxy. London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer. The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kiev’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”
Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, was asked during a visit to Wolverhampton bus station what his message to Vladimir Putin was. He said: “This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100% against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin.”
He added: “We are providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself, and that’s been the British position all the way through this conflict by previous prime ministers. It remains the case with me. We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.”
The Ministry of Defence had responded the previous evening, saying that Britain stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and is committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin’s illegal invasion.
The embassy statement followed reporting in the Sunday Times that Ukraine had used drones made by two British companies as part of its deep strike campaign. The embassy’s response was posted on its Telegram channel.
Ukraine has expanded long-range strikes against Russian territory considerably this year, with drones and missiles aimed at military industry, oil refineries and logistics. Data from the conflict monitor Acled indicates Ukraine launched three times as many such strikes in July as it did in January, and the campaign has forced Russia to spread its air defences across a far larger area.
Among the targets have been distribution depots belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, an approach aimed at cutting revenue funding the war and bringing its effects home to the Russian public. A strike last week hit a Wildberries logistics hub at Koledino in the Podolsk district, around 25 miles south of the Kremlin, during an attack the regional governor described as among the most massive in recent times.
The Russian defence ministry said on Saturday that it had shot down 598 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions, along with the Black and Azov Seas and Crimea.
Warnings of this kind from the Russian embassy in London are routine rather than exceptional, and the mission has issued similar statements on British sanctions, cyber measures and remarks by sports officials in recent weeks. Moscow made comparable accusations in 2022 over alleged British involvement in the drone attack on the Black Sea Fleet at Sevastopol, which Britain rejected at the time.
The two British companies named in the reporting have not commented publicly, and the government does not routinely confirm which specific systems it has supplied to Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia’s economy is growing faster than expected. It probably won’t last.
articles.body:
Russia’s economy is growing faster than expected. It probably won’t last.
Last week, Rosstat published seemingly encouraging news about the state of the economy: Russia’s GDP grew by 1.3% year-over-year in the second quarter, after shrinking by 0.2% in the first three months of 2026. This result even exceeded the expectations of the Central Bank of Russia and the Economic Development Ministry. But it’s too early to talk about the economy’s recovery: the quarterly growth was driven by temporary factors. Why is there little reason to expect the rebound to become a long-term trend? How did a sober analysis of Russia’s prospects lead to the dismissal of one of the country’s most respected economists? And what risks does the growing budget hole pose?
Why the economy grew in the second quarter — and what obvious problems remain
As noted above, temporary factors were largely behind the 1.3% GDP growth recorded in April–June 2026.
- The calendar. The second quarter had 5% more working days than the same period in 2025 — 62 compared with 59.
- Higher military and government spending. The federal budget spent 11.5 trillion rubles over those three months, up from about 10 trillion rubles in the second quarter of 2025, a roughly 13% increase. Government procurement, which includes the state defense order, jumped 38.5% compared with April–June of last year.
- Several sectors saw gains. Construction, for instance, narrowed its year-over-year decline to 1.6%, after plunging 10% in the first quarter. Growth in retail trade turnover doubled. Wholesale trade turnover returned to growth, up 2.4%, after falling 0.5% in January–March. The same held true for freight turnover.
Industrial output growth also accelerated in the second quarter, rising to 0.6% from 0.3% in the first. A military-industrial complex flush with orders is keeping the sector from contracting, while the decline in oil production and a slump in civilian industries are dragging it down. Those civilian sectors continue to struggle under the Russian central bank’s double-digit key rate of 14%, which the regulator can’t cut faster because inflation remains near 6% annually. Civilian manufacturing output excluding the oil industry fell 2.1% in June and remains nearly 4% below the 2024 monthly average, according to calculations by TsMAKP.
It’s worth noting that the effects of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries — which caused a gasoline shortage nationwide — and on warehouses belonging to Wildberries will likely only show up in third-quarter 2026 data.
After Rosstat published its data, the Economic Development Ministry raised its first-half GDP growth estimate from 0.3% to 0.6%. But it’s too early to draw broader conclusions from the trend: growth is likely to moderate in the second half of the year, since the rebound appears temporary, analysts at Raiffeisenbank believe.
In May, the Economic Development Ministry cut its 2026 GDP growth forecast threefold, from 1.3% to 0.4%. Russia’s central bank, in July, projected growth of 0-1%. That means the economy is unlikely to outperform 2025, when growth was limited to 1% after two consecutive years of growth above 4%, fueled by extraordinary military spending.
How talk of the economy’s problems became taboo — illustrated by the firing of Andrei Klepach as chief economist of the Russian state corporation VEB.RF
Andrei Klepach, a former deputy head of the Economic Development Ministry, was fired from his post as chief economist at VEB.RF after media outlets drew attention to remarks he made in May at a meeting of the Nikitsky Club at the Moscow Exchange. The dismissal underscored both the relevance of the economy’s current problems and the authorities’ reluctance to acknowledge the war as the main cause.
Klepach didn’t say anything radical — he simply stated the obvious. Half of the slowdown in economic growth, he said, stems from an extremely tight monetary policy that led to a decline in investment and, combined with reduced subsidized lending, slowed overall consumer demand:
I would say 50% [of the slowdown in economic growth] is due to the Central Bank; roughly 30%, though it’s hard to calculate precisely, is due to the Industry and Trade Ministry, because we’ve ceded most of the automotive and road machinery market to the Chinese. Chinese imports account for nearly 50% of the passenger car market, and including assembly, more than 70%; for trucks, it’s 60%.
Klepach listed a string of sector-specific problems: technological and design flaws in the new lineup of domestic planes in civilian aircraft manufacturing; weak demand in construction materials production and metallurgy; and shortages of raw materials alongside import dominance in light industry. And he warned: “Not all the barriers and costs are caused by the policy of Russia’s central bank; even with a substantial rate cut, there will be no rapid growth.”
Klepach forecast that the continuing war, persistent sanctions, and tight monetary and fiscal policy would keep the economy from growing faster than 2-2.5% a year. Russia won’t survive the competition in a protracted standoff with the West amid the risk of a social crisis at home, he concluded — and it cost him his job.
Whatever we do with our economy, it will survive. In that sense, there’s no critical point from an economic standpoint. But there are losses — investment has fallen, there’s no growth, let alone productivity growth… […]
We’re falling behind. We’re losing both the technological and economic competition in the world. And… we’re losing it not only to China and the U.S., we’re losing it in some ways to Ukraine too, as unpleasant as that is for me to say.
Ukraine’s economy, of course, is partly destroyed, and there’s a demographic catastrophe. But, again, the Ukrainian economy, despite everything, is surviving. Of course, there’s enormous financial aid there, without which everything would have collapsed. With that kind of aid, military spending and their own spending amounts to almost 50% of our budget. And if you take all the aid as a whole, it’s many times more than our capital outflow. In other words, we’re financing the world, and the world is financing Ukraine. At least, the unfriendly Western world is.
So in this war of attrition, we won’t win the competition. We have this illusion that everything over there will collapse. It hasn’t collapsed and it won’t. Our costs are growing. According to public opinion surveys, the quality of healthcare is deteriorating for us. In the scientific and technological sphere, things are very uneven. In some areas we have results and breakthroughs, but overall, in my view, we’re losing the competition, not winning it.
Inequality problems are growing. After a substantial decrease in 2023–2024, everything is now moving in the opposite direction.
In my opinion, the economy will hold up, but a social crisis could arise, and precisely when no one particularly expects it. But let me remind you, no one expected the February Revolution either. […]
I believe Russia won’t fall apart, but I’m almost certain we’ll arrive at a social crisis. Economically we won’t collapse, but our lag will keep growing, with all the consequences that entails.
The deficit in the federal budget remains a problem for the authorities — and they have effectively run out of tools to fill state coffers
The rebound in GDP growth and the crackdown on public discussion of the economy’s problems can’t hide another problem: the federal budget deficit grew by 724 billion rubles in July, reaching 6.455 trillion rubles — 2.8% of GDP — since the start of the year. The cause is unchecked growth in military spending. Government procurement, which includes the state defense order, rose nearly 40% year-over-year from January through July, to 8.44 trillion rubles, already 80% of the annual plan.
Oil and gas revenues, meanwhile, fell almost 16.8%, to 4.6 trillion rubles. The damper mechanism “ate up” most of Russia’s “profit” from the war in the Middle East and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, while export infrastructure continues to suffer from Ukrainian military strikes.
The government is partly offsetting the shortfall with taxes on businesses and citizens: VAT revenue, boosted by a rate hike to 22%, jumped 25%, to 9.8 trillion rubles.
Economist Sergei Aleksashenko, a former deputy chair of Russia’s central bank and deputy finance minister, believes the total federal budget deficit for 2026 could reach 7–7.5 trillion rubles. That estimate matches the expectations of the chief economist at a Russian analytical center who spoke with Meduza.
The question is how to close that hole, equivalent to about 3% of GDP. The Finance Ministry doesn’t have many tools left. From January through July, it raised 2.3 trillion rubles by borrowing on the domestic debt market through OFZ bonds, which state banks buy up — but was forced to halt bond placements because of high rates of around 16%. Servicing domestic debt, in other words, has become very costly for the budget: it’s already the fifth-largest line item in planned federal spending, almost 9% of GDP.
The Finance Ministry also took nearly 460 billion rubles from the National Wealth Fund, received about 200 billion rubles from the sale of nationalized assets, and financed another 3.5 trillion rubles by drawing down Treasury funds held in bank accounts and other monetary instruments.
Foreign capital markets remain closed to Russia, so there are effectively no tools left to finance the deficit: borrowing even more domestically or draining the National Wealth Fund further means a risk of inflation in an economy already overheated by the fuel crisis. “The most unlikely scenario is that the Finance Ministry agrees to cut the pool of free Treasury funds even further (a little more than 4.5 trillion rubles remain),” Aleksashenko said.
All these economic and budgetary problems will ultimately hit ordinary Russians, as Andrei Klepach warned in his now-famous remarks. Growth in real disposable income could amount to a mere 0.6% in 2026, and inequality has stopped declining: pensions are falling further behind wages, while tax increases are squeezing small and medium-sized businesses, the economist said.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: UAE says it detected 2 incoming ballistic missiles launched from Iran
articles.body:
Serdar Dincel
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) Defense Ministry on Tuesday announced that the country's air-defense systems had detected two ballistic missiles launched from Iran.
 
Assessments show that the missiles "were targeting maritime navigation and fell into the sea," the ministry said in a statement on US social media company X.
 
In an earlier statement, the ministry said the UAE “remains fully prepared and ready to respond to any threats, and to firmly counter any attempts to undermine the country’s security.”
 
Tensions in the Middle East have heightened after the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran. In response, Tehran retaliated with strikes in regional countries, including the UAE, hosting US assets.
 
In mid-June, Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding under Pakistani mediation aimed at ending their war and reaching a lasting peace agreement.
 
Talks, however, have since broken down amid ongoing disputes over the memorandum’s terms and navigation through the Hormuz Strait, a critical route for global energy exports.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Seven Russian Military Targets, Including Five UAV Command Posts
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Strikes Seven Russian Military Targets, Including Five UAV Command Posts
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck several Russian military targets on August 17 and overnight into August 18, including an ammunition depot and multiple drone command posts, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian forces targeted an ammunition depot near Karlivka in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, the General Staff reported.
Five Russian UAV command posts were also struck during the operation. Two were located near Ustinka and Zhuravlivka in Russia’s Belgorod region, while three others were targeted near Novoivanivka, Nove, and Mali Shcherbaky in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region.
In addition, Ukrainian forces struck a separate Russian command post near Terny in the Donetsk region.
The strikes come amid a broader series of Ukrainian operations targeting Russian military infrastructure and logistics. On August 17, Ukraine’s 1st Azov Corps of the National Guard reported another large-scale drone operation against Russian fuel infrastructure and military logistics in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region.
According to Azov, the strikes completely destroyed facilities used to store and supply fuel to Russian troops. The corps also released footage showing attack drones hitting fuel storage sites across the occupied part of the Donetsk region.
The operation followed another series of strikes overnight on August 16, when Ukrainian forces targeted Russian military and logistics facilities, including a railway bridge used for military logistics, ammunition and supply depots, and a missile unit.
