articles.title: ‘I want to hug an actual, living person’: How Meduza’s Russian readers are coping with wartime loneliness
articles.body:
‘I want to hug an actual, living person’: How Meduza’s Russian readers are coping with wartime loneliness
In August, Meduza published a piece on how the war in Ukraine has caused an epidemic of loneliness in Russia. The people we spoke to described how the invasion destroyed their ties with relatives and friends and how everyday contact with the people around them disappeared from their lives. In that article, we asked Meduza’s Russian readers to share their own stories of loneliness and isolation, as well as how they cope with it. We are publishing some of the responses.
Caution: this text contains profanity. If that isn’t something you want to read, please skip it.
Alexander
Miass, Chelyabinsk region
My circle of friends is unrecognizable now, mostly because before 2022 I didn’t really have opinions about what was happening. When the [full-scale] war started, many of the people I talked to supported it, saying that was exactly what needed to happen — kill, bomb, whatever it took. Running into those same people now, in 2026, I see exhaustion in their eyes. They clearly want to get it off their chest. They want it to stop.
The only people I discuss the war and the whole fucking mess in this country with are my sister and her husband. We see things the same way. We don’t talk about how bad things are for Ukrainians — you can’t feel sorry for everyone, you can’t sympathize with everyone, there isn’t enough strength for that. Instead we’re trying to figure out how to keep living: what to do, how to accept the rules of the game and start playing by them even when they don’t suit you, how to adapt, where to cut corners.
I feel terrible, but life has to go on. I still have goals — a wedding, a child — but they keep getting pushed back because the politics and the economics make it hard. It needs to happen anyway, because I want it so much. So I try to “hit the right notes” [adapt to what’s going on].
Young people and older ones alike — anyone who just wants to live in peace, build up the country, and not fight with anyone — have had it drilled into us that holding different views costs you your freedom. I’ve already lost my moral freedom.
Igor
Volga region
It was clear right away, in February 2022, that reality had shifted — what had been allowed no longer was.
Conversations with people often ended relationships. I stopped talking to everyone from the older generation. It was like a crack splitting a rock.
Psychology has a concept called separation from one’s parents. Mine happened on an accelerated timeline — separation from my actual parents, and from the idea, hammered into us since childhood, that “society and the state are your parents.” I realized I’d stopped counting on outside help. If I got into an accident, for instance, I no longer expected anyone to come save me. That pushed me toward defensive life planning — risk management. You start leaving the house the way a peasant heads into the forest: a hostile, dangerous place where the best strategy is to grab what you need and get back out, if you want to keep living.
Then I realized that if I kept feeling responsible for everything, playing the good Samaritan the way I used to, I’d burn out and stop functioning — there’s simply too much evil around. So I gradually grew callous. My zone of responsibility shrank to 100 square meters (1,076 square feet) and three living creatures.
News that someone died somewhere no longer gets a reaction out of me. They died. We haven’t, not yet. If I die, everyone else will be just as indifferent, and that’s fine.
I had to stop communicating in Russian online. At some point it hit me that the man at the top had privatized the language. It’s his now, not mine — he decides what can and can’t be said in it. So screw him, I thought, let him choke on it. I’ve stopped consuming almost all Russian-language content, because nothing honest can come out of a privatized language, and I’m not even going to look for it. The one exception is a short list of outlets, including Meduza, which I keep around for warnings about imminent dangers.
In the end I started talking exclusively to foreigners, on foreign platforms, in English. There you barely have to censor yourself, though you do have to stay mindful of their own sensitive topics. That’s hard. But in some ways it’s easier — compared to the police, being cancelled is nothing, and the cost of a mistake is lower.
When ChatGPT entered my life in 2025, I felt enormous relief. Finally there was something that could sustain a discussion — probably better than anyone I know — without taking offense, while helping me refine and clarify my model of the world through dialogue. Now I can do that without other people, and without risking that someone will inform on me.
I’m essentially waiting for a technological revolution that will render today’s problems irrelevant, make countries and states redundant, and genuinely expand every individual’s capabilities. I’m waiting for the day the need to communicate directly with other people disappears entirely, because we don’t know how anymore and don’t want to learn.
I, for one, definitely don’t want to anymore. I’d rather hand my thoughts to an AI agent and let it discuss everything with the equivalent agent belonging to another person or organization. Let there be a layer like that, one capable of smoothing over the rough edges. Communication should be handled by an entity without a limbic system.
A decade or two from now, we’ll all be embarrassed to remember that we were even capable of waging war and squeezing each other economically over borders and flags nobody cares about — the way we now look back on the Crusades. But knowing a little more about humanity by then, we won’t talk about it. We’ll just pretend the 2020s never happened.
I no longer accept the concept of the nation-state at all. We don’t live on Earth, or in Europe or Asia, or in some particular nation-state — we live in a city or a village. Some people never venture beyond a few courtyards their whole lives.
I don’t want to fix a broken state. We’ve already spent decades trying and haven’t succeeded. It’s like an old car — at some point it’s simpler to send it to the junkyard and replace it with something conceptually new.
Andrey
Moscow
Before the [full-scale] war I had a large circle of friends and socialized constantly. Most of my closest friends scattered to different countries once the war and the mobilization began.
I didn’t leave — I have an elderly mother, and she has no one but me. Besides, I don’t speak any foreign languages and have no idea what I’d even do abroad.
I’ve always been interested in politics and tried to stay involved for as long as it was possible. Even if I could move to another country, I’d have no way to take part in political life there, and that doesn’t exactly make me want to leave.
To keep from losing my mind, I spent a couple of years on antidepressants after the war started, and thanks to them I quit drinking entirely. I decided that if I didn’t quit, I’d drink myself to death. Not long after February 24, the war had already claimed a friend of mine who couldn’t cope psychologically, started drinking, and, because of the alcohol, failed to give himself his insulin shot in time. He died.
Now I have to economize on antidepressants. I’m a freelancer in video production, and there’s less and less work, so I can’t afford a good therapist anymore. Going to the psychiatric clinic is terrifying.
I’ve had to cut ties with a bunch of people over their views since the war started. With some relatives and colleagues I now keep contact to a minimum. Only a handful of people are left with whom I can freely discuss what’s happening in the country.
The gist of it: I’ve retreated into internal emigration, just like Brodsky. I rarely leave the house except for work meetings with clients. You walk out of your building, see a poster for United Russia, tear it down — and a week later it’s back up again.
Spending so much time alone at home, I’ve gone back to playing video games the way I did as a teenager. Neural networks help keep me from losing my mind — I use them to dig into topics like the biography of Valentin Sokolov. It’s sad that I couldn’t find a single documentary about him, and I hope to make one myself someday. I also sometimes ask AI to talk with me as if it were a psychologist. And AI sex chats fill the loneliness that comes with not having relationships with women.
Anonymous reader
Moscow
I’m generally a solitary person, but once the [full-scale] war started I felt a much sharper need to find people like myself. I read people like me on Facebook, sure, but that’s not the same — I want to hug an actual, living person.
I can’t help myself — I throw probing, often careless remarks at everyone I run into: cab drivers, workers at pickup points, people I share an elevator with. My husband complains, but I can’t resist. For me it’s a kind of homemade sociology. I really want to know what’s going on in society.
Igor
Perm
I was living in St. Petersburg when the [full-scale] war started, but moved back to Perm in 2024 for family reasons.
Things are very bad here. In St. Petersburg I’d had a small antiwar circle of friends, but that disappeared the moment I moved. Now I’m immersed in an atmosphere of total support for the war — here it’s as natural as the weather. Whether what’s happening is “right” isn’t even up for discussion. What people do discuss is the deaths of mutual acquaintances (heroic ones, of course), weapons, new drones, “the West’s cunning plans.”
Neighbors greet SVO soldiers with vodka and snacks and sing at the top of their lungs until morning. Volunteers sewing camouflage netting look for helpers, and find them. Schoolkids run around the streets teasing each other: “You’re a Ukrainian — no, you are — no, you are — Ukrainian, Ukrainian, Ukes.” War and hatred are welded into the minds of people in this region.
Finding antiwar-minded people here is simply unrealistic. I feel locked in a prison of fear. All I have left is my family, who share my views — we’ve walled ourselves off and cut contact with the outside world, relatives included.
Changing the situation is practically impossible. I can’t leave, mainly for financial reasons, and I can’t leave my parents behind either. All that’s left is to accept it and wait. Real life is over. All that’s left is its empty shell.
Anonymous reader
There’s almost no one to discuss the war with anymore. Even everyday concerns and worries have become hard to talk about the way they used to be. I feel loneliness, deep sadness, powerlessness.
I discuss it with my therapist and with my boyfriend, though he’s not fully engaged — mostly I’m just venting. I try to spend time relaxing in nature and being around animals to cope with my psychological state. I keep my hope alive, do what I have to, and take small steps toward peace.
Alexander
Moscow region
In February 2022, when it all began, I was in the middle of changing my life — I’d taken a new job in a different field and made a lot of new acquaintances. I remember thinking: “This is going to be hard now, not just because I’m an introvert but because of what’s happening. How am I supposed to get along with new people if they’re “Za”? What if my new boss turns out to be one of them?”
But, strangely enough, no. I joined a large Telegram chat for specialists in my field from all over Russia, scrolled through the pinned messages, and found that people were horrified — but there were no war supporters there, or at least none who made themselves visible. When outright “Z-patriots” do wander in, they’re quickly shown the door. Back at the start of the war, some of the pinned messages were even strikingly respectful, along the lines of: “Given the latest news, let’s support our colleagues in Ukraine.”
I’ve since run into the same thing offline. I’m a freelancer who works with a lot of people and projects, and I go to gatherings now and then — everywhere it’s the same consensus. We either don’t mention the topic at all, or we bring it up cautiously, sadly, calling it “the trouble.” At business meetings and at parties alike, no one ever talks about the war directly, but from the averted eyes and the muttering through gritted teeth, I can tell everyone finds it deeply repulsive. A few times I got bolder and spoke more directly about it in private conversations, and every time, people clearly backed me up.
I’ve realized I’m surrounded by a lot of people who have both a heart and a functioning brain — more of them than I expected. When someone who supports the war does turn up, which is rare, I try to wrap up the conversation quickly. Trying to change their mind is both pointless and dangerous.
Alexander
Volzhsky, Volgograd region
My circle of friends shrank sharply, but I put that down to moving — I lived in Moscow from 2019 to 2023, then went back to my hometown.
At the start of the war, my close friends and I discussed it constantly. Then half of them left the country, though, to be fair, almost all of them later came back. Now I only discuss the topic openly with my fiancée, and even then only at home and quietly. I’m glad she shares my views.
I like to think I’m changing the situation. I try to be kind even to aggressive people, though it doesn’t always work since I can be harsh myself. People latch onto that these days, I think, and it makes them happy. I get the sense that people are tired of violence, rudeness, militarism, and all the other crap on TV — tired of the government’s rhetoric. But at the same time, it doesn’t seem to take much these days for a person in Russia to slide into hatred, violence, and radicalism. Then again, maybe I’m just judging by myself.
Polina
Ryazan
My circle of friends hasn’t changed since the [full-scale] war started, but my husband and I have gotten very careful about how we phrase things around people who support it. We don’t bring up the topic with our closest friends — we know where they stand, and we don’t want to lose friendships that go back years.
It’s a relief that my husband and I support each other and see things the same way. Without his support it would be hard, and I’d definitely feel lonely. My mother used to support all this “hype,” but she’s gradually starting to see the truth, which makes me very happy.
I try to focus on life’s small things — good food, new clothes, pleasant moments with loved ones, short trips to nearby towns. I do a bit of volunteering, helping clear the city’s riverside embankment along with other people who care. Some part of me is looking for a way to protest safely, but I haven’t found one yet.
Veronika
Moscow
I don’t really have friends anymore. In 2022 and 2023 I talked to people about the war constantly, trying to change their minds, and at some point it stopped seeming to mean anything. Now it’s just become awkward to even bring up the topic.
I managed to change my fiancé‘s mind, but no one else’s. I went to see [Boris] Nadezhdin, to vote in the [March 2024 presidential] election, to the Solovetsky Stone, to [Alexey Navalny’s] grave. I just loved being around people like me, watching them, even in silence — glad at how different they are and how many of them there are.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Russian missile strike hits center of Pechenihy in Ukraine’s northeastern Kharkiv Region, killing 10 and wounding 17
articles.body:
A Russian missile strike on the town of Pechenihy in Ukraine’s Kharkiv Region on the morning of Aug. 18 killed 10 people and wounded 17 others, according to a report by regional military administration head Oleh Syniehubov. Ukrainian authorities said the strike hit the center of the town, where cafes, a post office, and shops are located.
Fourteen of the wounded were hospitalized, while three others received treatment at the scene, Viktor Zabashta, director of the regional emergency medical center, told Suspilne, Ukraine’s public broadcaster. The wounded suffered burns and shrapnel injuries, and some are in serious condition. Syniehubov said DNA testing would be needed to identify the dead.
Oleksandr Husarov, head of the Pechenihy community, said Russian forces attacked the town with two Banderol missiles. The two munitions landed about 50 meters apart, with one striking a cafe. Among those killed, Husarov said, were customers, vendors, and people who were nearby. Work to clear the rubble is continuing, meaning the casualty figures could rise.
The attack damaged 10 private homes, a cafe, a post office, a shop, and at least seven cars. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the strike hit a “crowded intersection” surrounded by residential buildings. A fire at the site was extinguished.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, classifies the S8000 Banderol as a Russian cruise missile that is developed and produced by the Russian company Kronshtadt. It has a range of up to 500 kilometers and a maximum speed of 620 to 650 kilometers per hour. Among other components, the missile uses a Chinese turbojet engine and foreign-made electronics.

articles.title: US, Canada hold last-minute talks to stop 50% U.S. tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods
articles.body:
US and Canada hold last-minute talks to stop Trump’s 50% tariffs
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. and Canada are negotiating in an effort to reach a truce on tariffs before a 12:01 a.m. Wednesday deadline set by U.S. President Donald Trump.
If no deal is reached, Trump has threatened to impose 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian products, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Trump have spoken twice by phone in the past two days about the ongoing negotiations, including another call Tuesday afternoon, Carney’s office said, underscoring the last-minute push for a deal.
″We are negotiating,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Monday, speaking in French. “The negotiations are very intense and delicate. This is not the time to talk about negotiations in public.”
The two countries have wrangled for decades over trade, poking each other over sore spots like Canadian softwood lumber imports and U.S. access to Canada’s protected dairy market.
Somehow they still managed to remain friends, allies and trading partners. Canadian soldiers fought alongside Americans in Afghanistan after 9/11. The 5,525-mile U.S.-Canada border is undefended, and nearly 330,000 people and $2 billion worth of goods cross it every day; 800,000 Canadians live in the United States.
Trump’s approach to dealing with Canada marks an extraordinary departure from the traditionally cooperative relationship between the two countries. Trump has hit Canadian goods with tariffs — in a push to bring manufacturing back to the U.S. — and has repeatedly made inflammatory comments about turning Canada into America’s 51st state.
The Canadian public is fed up. A petition to expel the U.S. ambassador, a Trump ally, has collected nearly 218,000 signatures since July 21. It accuses Ambassador Pete Hoekstra of having “normalized’’ Trump’s talk of annexing Canada, among other complaints.
Looking for an off-ramp
Nearly 72% of Canada’s goods exports last year went to the United States. And the Trump administration might be wary of imposing a hefty new tariff — paid by U.S. importers who try to pass along the cost to consumers via higher prices — ahead of November’s midterm elections. U.S. voters are already frustrated with the high cost of living.
“I don’t think either side really wants these tariffs to come into effect,’’ said Ryan Majerus, a partner at King & Spalding and a former U.S. trade official. “There’s a pretty strong push on both sides to find an off-ramp here.’’
Majerus said the United States is aiming to get Canada to buy more U.S. military equipment, including F-35 fighters; to take part in Trump’s “Golden Dome’’ missile defense; and to give the United States more access to critical minerals, thereby reducing America’s reliance on tenuous supplies from its geopolitical rival, China.
The Canadians would like relief from U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum as well as softwood lumber, which the U.S. says receives unfair government subsidies.
Trump relies on Smoot-Hawley to go after Canada
Trump has made tariffs the centerpiece of his second-term economic agenda. Last year, he imposed double-digit import taxes on almost every country, justifying them by declaring the longstanding U.S. trade deficit a national emergency. The Supreme Court in February ruled that he’d overstepped his authority, striking down those tariffs and setting the stage for the federal government to pay refunds to importers.
Trump immediately looked for other ways to rebuild his tariff wall. Last month, he imposed import taxes of 10% to 12.5% on 59 countries and the European Union — which together account for 99% of U.S. imports — for allegedly failing to have or to enforce restrictions on imports made from forced labor.
Then he reached back to the Great Depression to find a cudgel with which to whack Canada.
Trump invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose 50% tariffs on products that account for about 5% of Canadian exports to the United States.
Nearly a century ago, with the U.S. and world economies in collapse, Congress passed the 1930 tariff law, imposing hefty taxes on imports from around the world. Known as the Smoot-Hawley tariffs, named for their congressional sponsors, they are notorious among economists and historians for limiting world commerce and making the Great Depression worse.
Section 338 tariffs have never been used before. U.S. trade negotiators traditionally have favored another tool, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 — the provision Trump invoked to impose last month’s forced-labor tariffs.
Section 338 authorizes the president to impose tariffs of up to 50% on imports from countries that have discriminated against U.S. businesses. Unlike Section 301 sanctions, no investigation is required. Nor is there any limit on how long the tariffs can stay in place.
In announcing the Section 338 tariffs, Trump claimed that Canada discriminates against American exports of autos, alcohol and cheese. Trump is angry because Canada and China were the only countries that punched back with retaliatory tariffs of their own when he slapped levies on their products last year.
“If a country retaliates against us, we’re obviously not going to tolerate that,” U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters Friday at the Iowa State Fair. “We’ll take action. My sense is the Canadians, they want to have a more conciliatory approach, but we’ll see.”
New leverage to renegotiate USMCA
The U.S. is renegotiating a North American trade pact — the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement — that Trump strong-armed America’s neighbors into accepting in his first term. The threat of Section 338 tariffs gives the United States leverage to seek fresh concessions from Ottawa.
“From Carney’s perspective, you need (USMCA) to be renegotiated,” said Christopher Gundermann, a fellow in the economics program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “You can’t renegotiate it with a massive trade war going on.’'
But the Canadian public’s furor over Trump’s policies may limit Carney’s ability to cut a deal. Canada could retaliate again if the new 50% tariffs take effect, potentially aggravating a trade fight.
Canada’s government “cannot look like it is simply caving to the Trump administration’s demands,’’ said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal.
“Making further concessions without getting something meaningful in exchange would probably lead to a strong backlash ... The risk is for the Carney government to make Canada look weak and, therefore, even more vulnerable to future trade and geopolitical bullying on the part of the Trump administration.”
Dominic LeBlanc, Canada’s minister for U.S. trade, met with Greer on Monday. He was tight-lipped afterward.
“The work is continuing,’’ he said. “We continue to do our job.’’
____
Gillies reported from Toronto.

articles.title: Israel strikes NE. Syria's abandoned Abu al-Duhur air base
articles.body:
Israel carried out a series of airstrikes on northeastern Syria's Abu al-Duhur military air base Tuesday, according to Syrian state media and a war monitor.
The attack on the disused air base came after a recent visit to the site by a Turkish delegation.
Israel has been carrying out incursions into Syrian territory since the December 2024 overthrow of longtime ruler Bashar Assad, including sending troops into a U.N.-patrolled buffer zone that separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights since 1974.
It has also hit key military sites including several airfields, according to the U.K.-based war monitor, Syrian Observatory for Human Rights.
"Israeli occupation aircraft early this morning targeted the runway ... with eight strikes," Syrian state television quoted an unidentified military source as saying.
It added that "the attack resulted in material damage to the airport's infrastructure, without causing casualties."
The facility has been out of service since 2012 and is currently protected by Syrian Defense Ministry forces, a security source told Agence France-Presse (AFP), without reporting any casualties.
According to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, the strikes came after "a visit by a Turkish military delegation to the airfield in recent days as part of efforts to reactivate it."
Türkiye is a key ally of the new government in Damascus.
No side has claimed the strikes on the airfield and the Israeli military said "no comment" in response to an AFP inquiry about the strikes.
A U.S.-led international coalition against the Daesh terrorist group has previously carried out strikes on senior terrorist figures in the northwest.
Syria is now part of the coalition.
Israel has launched hundreds of strikes on Syria since the fall of Assad and Israeli officials have said they intend to keep forces in a "security zone" in southern Syria, where they seek a broader so-called "demilitarized zone."
Damascus has repeatedly condemned incursions in the country's south.
During a joint press conference with his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron in Damascus last month, Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa called for an "active French role" to halt Israeli escalations in his country.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani also last month condemned "the continuation of Israeli military actions" and warned that "the unlawful occupation of our land beyond the 1974 line is a direct threat to the security of the region."
He demanded an "immediate and unconditional withdrawal."
But last week Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said that his country planned to keep troops in Syria.
Israel captured most of the Golan from Syria in the 1967 Arab-Israeli War and later annexed the areas under its control, in a move not recognized by most of the international community.
The incursions have been condemned by the United Nations chief as "violations of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity."
Despite tensions between the neighbors, Israel and Syria's new authorities have held several rounds of direct talks and have agreed to establish an intelligence-sharing mechanism.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in June denied that his country sought to intervene militarily in Lebanon, where Israel is raising a separate war, after U.S. President Donald Trump suggested Damascus could get involved.
Hezbollah fought alongside Assad in the country's civil war, making al-Sharaa and the new authorities who toppled the former leader in 2024 deeply hostile to the group.
Syria's war shattered the country's infrastructure and pushed millions of people to flee internally and abroad.

articles.title: Russia weaponizes Ukrainian children in occupied territories. Ukraine singles out those responsible
articles.body:
Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) has named 10 people and two institutions it says are teaching Ukrainian children under occupation to handle weapons—and preparing them to serve Russia.
HUR says those named use youth groups, occupation education authorities, and schools to erase children’s Ukrainian identity and prepare them for Russian military service. Publishing their names supports Ukraine’s efforts to document the system and hold its organizers accountable, but HUR announced no charges or sanctions with the update.
How Russia militarizes Ukrainian youth in occupied territory
At a May 2026 “Zarnitsa 2.0” competition, the Kremlin-backed Movement of the First taught children to handle weapons and explosives and operate drones, HUR said.
At the competition’s stage in occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast, regional organizer Viktoria Kostromina stated those skills would provide children with a “reliable foundation in life.”
The training sits inside a much larger school system. From 1 September, occupation schools will add a separate basic military-training track alongside a new Russian ideology class and behavior grades. More than 582,000 children across nearly 2,000 schools study under the imposed Russian curriculum, according to the Almenda Center of Civil Education.
Russia is also embedding combat preparation more deeply. “Cossack classes” will make ideological and combat-related drills compulsory for fifth-graders in four occupied Donbas cities. In Crimea, occupation authorities say they have built a pipeline that selects schoolchildren for drone training and ultimately for the Russian military reserve.
The policy has a long horizon. Putin’s 2025 strategy set a 95% “Russian civic identity” target for occupied populations by 2036.
Who HUR says is behind the indoctrination
HUR linked the individuals to the Movement of the First, Yunarmia, occupation education bodies, and a school in Simferopol.
Whom the HUR identified
- Artur Orlov: chairman of the Kremlin-backed Movement of the First.
- Oleksii Lavrentiev, Marina Tsvetinskaya, Ruyal Aliyev, Ekaterina Kozyr, Viktoria Kostromina and Kateryna Popova: regional Movement of the First organizers in occupied Ukraine.
- Svitlana Bespalova: occupation deputy education minister in Crimea.
- Nikita Polyakov: Yunarmia organizer in occupied Kherson Oblast.
- Dmytro Pryvidion: director of School No. 5 in occupied Simferopol.
HUR also identified two institutions: Pryvidion’s School No. 5 and the Selet–Ak Bars youth center in Foros. It says the school holds militaristic activities and produces devices for loading rifle magazines, while the center stages pro-war events for children.
All 12 entries now appear in the “Child Kidnappers” section of HUR’s War&Sanctions database.
Ukraine has previously pursued individual organizers through criminal cases. In 2024, the SBU accused a Crimea occupation official of using schools and military camps to indoctrinate pupils and encourage enlistment in Russia’s forces.
Ukraine’s ombudsman later asked the ICC and Ukrainian law enforcement to recognize systematic child militarization as a crime against humanity.

articles.title: "We will be there in Ukraine's hour ‌of ⁠need": UK rejects Kremlin threats over drone supplies
articles.body:
"We will be there in Ukraine's hour of need": UK rejects Kremlin threats over drone supplies
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said London will support Ukraine 100% against Russia and remain by its side "in its hour of need" after Moscow warned London of "consequences" over drone supplies to Kyiv.
Source: Reuters, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Burnham said the UK is "doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100% against this illegal war" led by Russian ruler Vladimir Putin.
Quote from Burnham: "We are not fair-weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine's hour of need, and that won't change."
Details: Ukraine uses drones to carry out long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and logistics facilities.
The UK's Ministry of Defence has not confirmed whether British-made drones have been used in these strikes.
In June, the UK said it would supply Ukraine with 150,000 drones by the end of 2026 as part of a £752 million (US$996 million) funding package.
Background:
- Russia has accused the UK of "deliberately seeking escalation" after reports in the media said British-made drones had been used in strikes on targets inside Russia.
- In late July, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Burnham held their first meeting aboard an aircraft carrier stationed at the British naval base in Portsmouth.
- Burnham also announced that London would provide Ukraine with technology to protect Ukrainian drones.
- In early August, the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office announced an expansion of sanctions against Russia, adding 19 more entities to its sanctions list.

articles.title: Russia may introduce covert coercive measures instead of mobilization – CCD
articles.body:
Russia may introduce covert coercive measures instead of mobilization – CCD
Andrii Kovalenko, head of the Center for Countering Disinformation at Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council, said this in a Telegram post, Ukrinform reports.
"A number of economists in Russia and some political elites continue to advise Putin against announcing mobilization. Closed-door polling conducted weekly by Putin's administration across the regions also indicates a lack of public support for such a move. Instead, the possibility of covert coercive measures to increase the share of people signing contracts is being considered," he said.
According to Kovalenko, Putin wants mobilization, but carrying it out could undermine the existing social contract between the Russian authorities and the population. The war is generally perceived as something distant from most Russians, while participation in it is associated with financial compensation.
"Simply put, it is life in exchange for money. Mobilization would destroy this arrangement," Kovalenko said.
At the same time, he said Putin does not plan to end the war at least until 2028 and is already drawing up plans for military operations throughout 2027. However, not everyone supports these ambitions, meaning there is still room to influence Moscow.
"There are tools to exert such influence – our strikes on the Russian economy, EU support, all multiplied by the will of the United States and China," Kovalenko said.
He noted that this room for influence is limited but not hopeless. At the same time, he said, it is important for Ukraine to maintain internal unity, as Russia will devote significant resources not only to the battlefield but also to the information and political spheres.
"They will support certain potential political [projects] in Ukraine, bringing money into the country and looking for leaders. This track has not gone away," Kovalenko concluded.
Photo: Center for Countering Disinformation

articles.title: Why is the US ramping up Tomahawk production?
articles.body:
Inside Story
Why is the US ramping up Tomahawk production?
The Pentagon has contracted a defence manufacturer to increase the output of cruise missiles.
It’s a multibillion-dollar deal that some military analysts say confirms suspicions that the United States is running out of critical munitions.
The Pentagon has contracted defence company Raytheon to significantly increase its output of Tomahawk missiles.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Will Pakistan-Saudi-Turkiye alliance actually create a new regional order?
- list 2 of 3The Mecca pact is not just another regional alliance
- list 3 of 3Pentagon urges faster US weapons production amid stockpile concerns
Raytheon has supplied the US with weapons for decades, but this time is different.
The company is set to deliver the Tomahawks at an unprecedented scale and speed.
How important are these missiles to US defence strategy?
And could this ignite a global arms race – and lead to more conflict?
Presenter: Anna Burns-Francis
Guests:
David Des Roches – professor at the Thayer Marshall Institute and former Pentagon director for Arabian Peninsula affairs
Patrick Bury – defence and security specialist at the University of Bath and a former NATO analyst
Dan Grazier – senior fellow and director of the National Security Reform Program at the Stimson Center

articles.title: Pentagon demands audit of 30 universities, investigating Russian, Chinese, Iranian research ties
articles.body:
The US Defense Department formally notified 30 domestic academic institutions, directing them to immediately review their "academic, financial, and research collaborations with foreign entities of concern," the department announced on Monday.
The "foreign entities of concern" are defined as institutions listed under Section 1286 of the Fiscal Year 2019 National Defense Authorization Act, "as well as organizations associated with the rebranded Confucius Institutes," the Defense Department said.
The list includes 130 research institutes based in Russia, China, and Iran, including civilian universities.
The 30 US universities must "complete a comprehensive audit of all identified foreign collaborations, assess the exposure of sensitive or export-controlled research, and implement strict mitigation plans, including the termination of problematic partnerships," the department said. All findings must be submitted to the Defense Department by August 31, it said.
The department did not publicly name the 30 institutions. However, a US official listed the institutions to Fox News.
US universities under review includes Harvard, UC Berkeley, MIT, NYU, official tells FOX News
According to the official, the institutions are: Georgetown University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, University of California, Berkeley, University of California, San Diego, University of Texas at Austin, Emory University, Harvard University, Oklahoma State University, Penn State University, University of California, Los Angeles, University of Cincinnati, University of Minnesota, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, University of South Carolina, University of Southern California, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Bryant University, Cornell University, Drake University, Duke University, Illinois Institute of Technology, Johns Hopkins University, New York University, Northeastern State University, Tahlequah (Oklahoma), Portland State University, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale, Stony Brook University, University of Delaware, and University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign.
The department is making its efforts alongside "partners in Congress," including the "House and Senate Armed Services Committees, the House and Senate Appropriations Committees, and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party," it noted.
This coordination allows the Defense Department to "continue to build a robust research ecosystem that protects critical discoveries from exploitation," it added.
"This action is designed to protect American taxpayer-funded research investments from unauthorized technology transfer, intellectual property theft, and adversarial exploitation," the department said.
"The Department of War has zero tolerance for academic partnerships that compromise our national security," Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering, Emil Michael, said.
"Institutions that receive funding from American taxpayers must uphold the highest standards of research security, and these mandated audits will ensure accountability across the board," Michael added.
"Universities are critical partners in executing a wide range of Department of War research programs, and the Department must therefore ensure that our research investments are well protected from foreign exploitation," Assistant Secretary of War for Science and Technology, Dr. Joseph Jewell, said.
Since the start of fiscal year 2026, the Pentagon cannot fund "fundamental research" with any organization on the list. Under the 2026 National Defense Authorization Act, the Trump administration downgraded China to the US's second-ranked threat.
However, this recent clampdown comes amid ongoing intensity in the Pentagon's scrutiny of how China can use American research and technology to improve its military capabilities.
This includes a review of how China's military researchers used outputs from US artificial intelligence models to train domestic systems, published by Reuters in June.
US repeatedly investigating Harvard for ties to Chinese research, academics
Additionally, an investigation into Harvard University, which is one of the institutions named by the US official to FOX News, stated that Harvard failed to safeguard research collaborations with Chinese institutions, according to FOX.
The Ivy League school also allegedly received over $600m. from China under the federal Section 117 foreign-gift disclosure system, FOX reported. This would constitute more than any other US university, according to an Education Department dashboard cited in a report from the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.
Further, Harvard-affiliated researchers allegedly co-wrote work with academics from China's National University of Defense Technology, Beihang University, and Nanjing University of Science and Technology, as well as other Chinese institutions that are tied to the Chinese military, according to an investigation led by the Republican Party.
The investigation, reported by the South China Morning Post, a Hong Kong-based English-language outlet whose website is blocked in mainland China, cited the investigation, adding that the Republican Party's findings also accused Harvard of lacking the centralized infrastructure needed to identify and vet foreign research partnerships.

articles.title: Jason Arday’s death and the racist weaponisation of plagiarism
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Jason Arday’s death and the racist weaponisation of plagiarism
On 18 July 2003, the body of UK weapons scientist Dr. David Kelly was discovered in the woods of Oxfordshire, some twenty miles away from the library where I was then writing a doctorate about Iraq. His death was ruled a suicide.
23 years later, Dr Jason Arday was found dead in south London, a few days after resigning from the University of Cambridge over allegations that he copied another person’s thesis, including the typographical errors.
Both Kelly and Arday were named, pushed into the media spotlight, and destroyed.
I never met Kelly, but we sat in the same seat a few days apart during a UK parliamentary inquiry. I was summoned to Parliament in 2003 because the British government had plagiarised material from my thesis and copied it into a dossier that Colin Powell presented to the United Nations to justify the invasion of Iraq, including my typographical errors.
Ironically, I was an Anglo-American of Iraqi heritage whose research had inadvertently become part of the justification for the invasion of my ancestral homeland. I never needed convincing that plagiarism matters. Since 2003, I have been trying to convince public audiences that it does.
In my Newlines Magazine article, ‘From the Dodgy Dossier to the Cambridge Controversies, Not All Plagiarism Is Alike,’ I wrote about the 2023 case in which Claudine Gay, the first Black president of Harvard University in Cambridge, US, was the target of plagiarism allegations. In Cambridge, UK, Jason Arday was the youngest Black professor in the university’s history. While my work was linked to the Iraq War, they were targets in the culture war over Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI).
Plagiarism is a matter to be weaponised, and only the strong have the power to survive its attack. Rarely do those caught up in plagiarism cases survive the attack.
Nobody in Tony Blair’s government, as far as we know, was disciplined for the plagiarism, despite lengthy trials and testimonies, including the Hutton Inquiry. The UK government taught a lesson that plagiarism is survivable if you have power. The lesson from Gay and Arday’s death is that it is not survivable without power.
In Arday’s case, there is another connection to those without power. It is rarely asked if his neurodivergence was a factor in what played out, similar to the life of the mathematician John Nash, the Nobel Prize winner whose struggle with mental illness inspired the movie “A Beautiful Mind.”
In all three cases, plagiarism led to three academics leaving their university positions.
In my TEDx IE Madrid talk ‘The Dodgy Dossier, the Iraq War, and Me,’ I talk about how when I moved to Istanbul, Turkey, to take my first academic job in 2004, Turkish newspapers featured headlines tying me to the justification for the 2003 war, with some headlines calling me its architect or “mastermind.” Taxi drivers and fruit vendors asked me why I had started it.
At my university, leftist students organised protests against my presence and called me the architect of the Iraq War. In this case, it was weaponised by leftist students opposed to the Iraq War. Tragically, I agreed with them and told them so directly when they confronted me.
I had not plagiarised anyone, but rather I was the person plagiarised from, by a government whose war I opposed, using work I had written to explain to Saddam Hussein’s police state, which I also opposed. None of that mattered. Like the professors who followed me, a crowd decided my name did not belong in a lecture hall. They were not interested in learning the difference between the man who did the research and the government that stole it.
They have good reason to. As for the death of Dr. Kelly, this is how I most likely became a target in Turkey.
Another UK government report, issued in September 2002, falsely claimed that Iraq could deploy chemical munitions in 45 minutes. Kelly, a scientist in the UK Ministry of Defence and a commentator on a draft of that dossier, revealed to the BBC that the 45-minute figure was an exaggeration and asserted that Alistair Campbell, Blair’s media advisor, used that figure to “sex-up” the Iraqi WMD threat, giving the September 2002 dossier the title the “sexed-up dossier.”
My work was plagiarised in a February 2003 dossier known as the “dodgy dossier,” for which Campbell also took responsibility.
It was during the media frenzy in the UK that Kelly died by suicide. The dossiers became interchangeable in media reporting, and I argue they could collectively be labelled the “dodgy sex dossier.”
Those who did not follow the affair closely, including the Turkish media and students, associated me with the 45-minute claim. This conflation unleashed hostility toward me both in my personal and public lives, but nothing like that endured by Gay and Arday, who faced death threats and a barrage of racist tirades.
This precedent demonstrates that, over time, the nuances in these cases will be forgotten, with juries already having made up their minds.
I do not compare my life to the deaths of Arday or Kelly, or Gay’s resignation. My experience in Turkey led me to teach at IE University in Madrid and Segovia, which turned out to be a dynamic, cosmopolitan campus—a silver lining.
Yet all universities around the world need to have courses on plagiarism for both professors and students, especially in the age of artificial intelligence. The state universities in California where I work cite a lack of funding for these courses, but they have agreements with major AI and plagiarism tech companies. For years, I have approached these companies that make plagiarism software, telling them: “If you make money from selling this technology to universities, you can give back by teaching how to avoid plagiarism in the first place,” but to no avail.
Finally, bringing up the “dodgy dossier” should serve as a prominent reminder that civil society and the media need to remain vigilant. If the US and UK launched a war against Iraq in 2003 based on fabricated evidence, there should have been a greater uproar over the so-called intelligence that the US claimed to attack Iran in 2026.
Ibrahim Al-Marashi is an associate professor of Middle East history at California State University, on the board of the International Security and Conflict Resolution (ISCOR) program at San Diego State University, and a visiting faculty member at The American College of the Mediterranean and the Department of International Relations at Central European University. His publications include Iraq’s Armed Forces: An Analytical History (2008), The Modern History of Iraq (2017), and A Concise History of the Middle East (2024).
Follow him on Twitter: @ialmarashi
Have questions or comments? Email us at: editorial-english@alaraby.co.uk
